items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by The Understory . W hen I was a student at Cornell University, I read the book “Fraternity Gang Rape” by Peggy Reeves Sanday for one of my classes. That book was written in 1990, which was a long time ago. But then again, was it? I took the book off my shelf today. Paging through it, I noticed a sickening pattern. Parts of it felt ripped from the allegations coming out of the Cornell investigation today: Long nights saturated in alcohol. Women who spend days tunneling through layers of self-blame and shame before concluding they’ve been raped. Prosecutors who do not pursue charges. One example: a 19-year-old woman at a small Midwestern college drank alcohol, had sex with her boyfriend, “fell asleep and the next thing she knew she awoke with a man she didn’t know on top of her.” The more things change, apparently, the less any goddamn thing changes. But wait. At moments of despair like this, I have learned to stop and ask myself: Is it actually true that nothing has changed? There has been some extraordinary reporting done about the Cornell case, including by The Cornell Daily Sun , the student-run newspaper that gave me my first reporting job many years ago. But as usually happens with terrifying news stories, it’s very hard to figure out how to assess the threat — and find proven solutions. How typical was this case? Is sexual assault happening more or less over time? In other words, what is the denominator for whatever fresh horror we are worried about? Most importantly, what actually works to make sexual assault more rare? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] To answer these questions, I’m going to uncomfortably set aside many other important questions — about accountability, humanity, legality, fairness and barbarity. Those are questions being interrogated in many other places. Here at The Understory, we’re trying to fill gaps that we see in traditional journalism. And one of those gaps is almost always context: How often are horrible things happening, and what can be done to make them more rare? These are the kinds of questions that we know humans need answered, in order to stay sane and take meaningful action in a time of relentless news battering us from near and far. So in that spirit, here is what I have learned so far: Rape reports have been declining in the U.S. since 2021. For 2025, the FBI estimates that 36 rape offenses were reported for every 100,000 people. The number of rapes that get reported to law enforcement each year has been gradually declining every year since 2021 , based on FBI data. This data comes with giant caveats, though. First, the number of actual sexual assaults is far higher than the number that get reported. (Only about 24 percent of sexual assaults were reported to authorities in 2024, according to the National Crime Victimization Survey .) Second, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013, so it is hard to compare statistics going back any further than that. (The current definition includes “penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object, or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of the victim.”) In general, definitions of rape and sexual assault vary from place to place, making it harder than it should be to track changes over time and to find which cities, states or countries have unusually low (or high) rates. Sexual assault remains appallingly common on college campuses. In 2019, 13 percent of college students reported that they’d experienced some form of sexual assault since they’d arrived on campus. This category is broader than the FBI definition of rape; it includes nonconsensual penetration, attempted penetration, sexual touching by force or inability to consent. This data comes from the 181,752 students who responded to the 2019 Campus Climate Survey (conducted by the Association of American Universities). Importantly, the odds vary tremendously depending on who you are. The rate of sexual assault for women and transgender or nonbinary students was 20 percent — or four times the rate for men. Credit: Zhuoyao Song / Shutterstock The Cornell case is typical in some ways. In most campus sexual assaults, both the victim and the offender have consumed alcohol or drugs. Typically, rape victims are girls and very young women, and the vast majority of perpetrators are male. Victims usually know their perpetrators. At colleges, assaults primarily happen in residences or fraternity houses, according to the Campus Climate Survey (and Cornell’s own 2025 survey on sexual assault). And if a victim reports the offense, official responses are slow and unsatisfying, generally speaking. In all these ways, the Cornell case seems fairly typical. The Cornell case is atypical in other ways. Most sexual assault cases involve just one perpetrator, not multiple, making the Cornell allegations unusual. The other rarity is that the woman in this case reported the incident. And she has continued to push for a reckoning in a civil suit filed this year. To date, none of the accused men has been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing. Something can be done. And is being done. There is a lot of speculation happening right now about what leads to rape. Can we blame always-accessible, violent porn? Or campus hookup culture and frat-boy privilege? I have hunches about this, like everyone else. But I’m more interested in evidence of change. What actually works to reduce the number of rapes? And guess what? We now have some answers — answers we did not have when I was a student at Cornell. A 2014 study led by Laura Salazar at Georgia State University randomly assigned 743 college men to receive something called the RealConsent online training or a generic online health program. RealConsent featured six 30-minute modules about informed consent, intimate communication skills, the role of alcohol and male socialization in sexual violence, empathy for rape victims and bystander education. Six months later, the men who had received the special training reported intervening more often to stop a peer from engaging in sexually violent or inappropriate behavior. And, most importantly, they reported engaging in less sexual aggression themselves. “The odds for perpetrating among RealConsent participants were 73 percent lower than participants in the comparison condition,” according to the study. The attitudes of these men changed, too. They had greater empathy for rape victims, less hostility toward women and less comfort with other men’s inappropriate behaviors. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Another program, which has been studied even more extensively, first appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2015. The researchers, led by Charlene Senn at the University of Windsor, randomly assigned a group of first-year female students at three Canadian universities to receive a special training program for resisting sexual assault. The control group got general brochures on sexual assault instead. The training program, known as EAAA (for Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act) featured four three-hour sessions. Students were taught how to assess risk, overcome emotional barriers in acknowledging danger and engage in effective verbal and physical self-defense. In all, 451 women received the EAAA training, and 442 women got the brochures. One year later, the researchers checked in on the women. Get this: women in the training group were 46 percent less likely to report having been raped than women in the control group. They were also 63 percent less likely to report attempted rapes. A subsequent study found that the benefits continued, even two years later. “The program significantly reduced the risk of completed and attempted rape, attempted coercion, and nonconsensual sexual contact over the entire follow-up period,” the study concluded, “yielding reductions between 30 percent and 64 percent at 2 years.” Women who still became victims of sexual violence, despite the training, were less likely to blame themselves than women in the control group. The U.S. Air Force Academy has adopted the program for first-year female cadets. So have many colleges, including Stanford University. Interestingly, Cornell University has tried out this program, too. Cornell facilitators piloted the EAAA program in 2019 and 2020. Then the pandemic came along and on-campus training stopped . Which means it’s unlikely that the students involved in the 2024 case got this training. Last year, Cornell revived the EAAA program with sorority members, as well as a parallel program for fraternity members. You might wonder: Why isn’t every high school student getting proven training like this? There are many reasons, but one reason is that too few people know about these options. When rapes get covered in the media, the reporting almost never includes research like this. It can feel like this kind of violence is inevitable — or the fault of some inherent flaw in the perpetrators. But violence is never inevitable. We, as a society, tend to focus on holding perpetrators accountable after the fact. And this is important, but tragically late. It would be great if laws were clearer, data collection was consistent and police and prosecutors had excellent, trauma-informed training. But it would be infinitely better to prevent more rapes from happening at all. “Despair demands less of us, it’s more predictable, and in a sad way safer,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in Hope in the Dark. “Authentic hope requires clarity — seeing the troubles in this world — and imagination, seeing what might lie beyond these situations that are perhaps not inevitable and immutable.” The post There Are Ways to Reduce Campus Sexual Assaults. Will More Colleges Use Them? appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: For decades, rhino conservation in Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh was built around protected enclosures. The approach helped a population recover after the species had disappeared from the region, but the next question is harder: can these animals live, breed and survive as a genuinely free-ranging population within a functioning Terai landscape? That question is now being tested. In March 2026, four greater one-horned rhinos were moved out of Dudhwa's fenced rehabilitation area into suitable grassland habitat in the reserve. The release took the number of mature rhinos free-ranging in Dudhwa to eight. The state's longer-term plan is to explore the feasibility of having 10 rhinos free-ranging as an initial phase of a wider conservation strategy. The latest census, conducted in June 2026, counted 53 rhinos in Dudhwa: 17 adult males, 25 adult females and 11 calves older than one year. Eight of them were among those released from the rehabilitation enclosures to improve genetic diversity and reduce inbreeding. But the significance of Dudhwa is not simply that there are more rhinos here than there were four decades ago. It is that the reserve is now becoming a test ground for a much larger question: what does it take to move from reintroduction to a resilient rhino population that can sustain itself across the wider Terai? From five rhinos to a larger experiment Dudhwa's rhino story began in 1984, when five rhinos were brought in as part of a reintroduction programme . The population has since grown, demonstrating that the Terai can once again support the species. But numbers alone can conceal the harder ecological questions. A population can grow while remaining vulnerable to genetic limitations, habitat pressures, disease, predation or a lack of connectivity with other populations. For a large herbivore such as the greater one-horned rhino, a viable future depends on much more than a protected patch of land. Amit Sharma, National Lead, Rhino Conservation at WWF India, sees the current phase in Dudhwa as a shift in that direction. "It is a great achievement for rhino conservation in Dudhwa as the rhinos have been allowed free range outside the enclosed area after almost four decades. Even though the initial plans are to release 10 rhinos, the objective should be more than releasing the 10 rhinos — it should be establishing an ecologically functional, demographically viable and genetically resilient free-ranging rhino population." The test now is whether the landscape can support the next generation, and the one after that, without conservation managers having to intervene constantly. What does a rhino need from a landscape? The Terai is a landscape of grasslands, wetlands, swamps, rivers and forests. Rhinos depend heavily on productive grasslands and water, while the mosaic of habitats allows them to feed, wallow and move through the landscape. Dudhwa already has much of this. "Dudhwa already has a successful reintroduction history and the basic ecological foundation : extensive terai grasslands, wetlands, swamps and riparian habitats are already in place," Sharma says. He points to a 2022 analysis which estimated that around 20% of Dudhwa was under grasslands and another 3% under wetlands, marshes and swamps, habitat classes that are critical for a flourishing rhino population. But having these habitats on a map is only the beginning. Instead of asking how Dudhwa can maintain one population, planners may eventually need to ask how Dudhwa, Valmiki, Nepal's Terai and other suitable habitats can function as parts of a larger rhino landscape. Photograph: (WWF India) "The natural water flows must be maintained, and perennial water sources must be secured to maintain the habitat standards. Further, the grassland extent and quality also must be managed to support a good herbivore population, especially for a mega-herbivore like the rhino." That makes habitat management one of the central lessons of Dudhwa. A rhino recovery programme cannot be separated from the health of the grassland itself. If grasslands degrade or natural water flows are disrupted, simply adding more rhinos will not solve the problem. And so the experiment in Dudhwa is also about learning how to manage a landscape before attempting to expand a population beyond it. The real test begins after release There is another difference between rhinos in an enclosure and rhinos that range freely. Once animals move through a larger landscape, conservation managers have to understand where they go, what they eat, how they reproduce, which calves survive and what causes mortality. Sharma says this requires long-term monitoring rather than periodic population counts alone. "For long-term viability of the population through active management, it will be necessary to undertake systematic monitoring for individual identification, reproductive success, calf survival, mortality, home-range use, forage availability and genetic diversity. Non-invasive DNA and technology-based approaches can strengthen population monitoring." In other words, Dudhwa's success will need to be measured in biological terms. Are females producing calves? Are those calves surviving? Are animals using suitable habitat? Is the population genetically healthy? Are rhinos able to expand their range? And can the population continue growing without continual human supplementation? These are the indicators that could determine whether Dudhwa's experience can inform future conservation in the Terai. The landscape does not end at Dudhwa The Terai does not follow state boundaries, and wildlife does not recognise them either. Dudhwa sits within a wider ecological system connected to other forests and protected areas in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal. Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar is another important rhino landscape, while rhinos also move across the India-Nepal border. A 2025 Wildlife Institute of India study on the Western Terai Arc Landscape highlighted how roads, development and other land-use changes can disrupt wildlife corridors, affecting the movement of large mammals and potentially isolating populations. Research and modelling under the project have specifically examined rhino and tiger habitat connectivity, and the areas where linear infrastructure could interfere with movement. For rhinos, that connectivity has consequences beyond movement. (1/3) Four greater one-horned rhinos have been released into the wild at Dudhwa Tiger Reserve, taking the free-ranging population to eight and strengthening conservation in India's Terai landscape. @moefcc @DudhwaTR @ManpowerGroupIn @experisitindia #WWFIndia https://t.co/vBt5uekU30 — WWF-India (@WWFINDIA) March 24, 2026 "A landscape-level approach is essential for the long-term recovery of rhinos in the Terai," Sharma says. "Rhinos do not recognise administrative boundaries, and the Katerniaghat–Bardia and Valmiki–Chitwan systems are ecologically interconnected." He points to a pattern already visible on the ground. "Studies have confirmed rhino movement across the India–Nepal border as a natural process to meet ecological requirements. Rhinos from Nepal are observed across the border on the Indian side at Pilibhit, Katerniaghat and Valmiki almost regularly." That changes the conservation question Instead of asking how Dudhwa can maintain one population, planners may eventually need to ask how Dudhwa, Valmiki, Nepal's Terai and other suitable habitats can function as parts of a larger rhino landscape. "It is thus essential to consider the entire area as one conservation unit and manage the rhino population as one single metapopulation or rather as a rhino landscape in the terai belt." But connectivity is not the only challenge. The same landscape that can support rhinos is also under pressure from infrastructure, human activity and climate-related changes. "The omnipresent risk to any rhino population is the threat of poaching arising out of the demand for the rhino horn and, to some extent, its body parts in the international market," Sharma says. But he points to another risk that may become harder to manage because it affects the habitat itself. "However, the predicted risk is the impact that a rapid change in the climate can exert in the region, which can lead to widespread effects in the fragile Himalayan system; the recent floods in Nepal during 2026 are indicative of the likely impacts." For rhinos, climate change is therefore not an abstract future threat. Changes in rainfall, flooding and water availability can alter the grasslands and wetlands on which the species depends. "The habitats in the terai are already under stress due to degradation and any deviation from the climatic pattern may result in drastic changes in the composition and condition of the habitats that may put the survival of the rhinos at risk." Then there is the human landscape around these habitats. "Again, due to multiple developments in the border areas and expansion of human activities, the connectivity with Nepal facilitating safe and active movement of rhinos and wildlife is under increasing threat. Any blockage in the natural connectivity will pose a huge challenge for rhino conservation in the entire Terai region." That means expanding rhino populations will require more than habitat protection. It will also require communities to be part of the conservation landscape. What happens when rhinos meet tigers? Dudhwa has another lesson to offer, and it is less comfortable. In March 2026, a 30-year-old female rhino named Rajeshwari was found dead in a water body in the reserve, with a tiger on her carcass. A post-mortem confirmed that she had died from injuries sustained in the attack. Reports said two sets of tiger pugmarks were found near the site. The incident raised an obvious question: if Dudhwa is trying to build a larger free-ranging rhino population, what happens when those rhinos share the landscape with a strong tiger population? Sharma says predation is part of the ecological reality, but adult rhino predation remains unusual. Dudhwa sits within a wider ecological system connected to other forests and protected areas in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal. Photograph: (Indian Express) "Tiger is an apex carnivore in the Indian forest, and it is quite natural for them to prey even on large animals like the rhino or the elephant." "In a park like Kaziranga, where tiger presence ten years back was not that dense, yet the rhinos falling prey to them was not uncommon. However, tigers preying on a healthy adult rhino are relatively rare, as it has been observed that they mostly attempt to attack the calves." For Dudhwa, however, the demographic consequences matter. "Rhino predation by tigers is not new to Dudhwa, and the death of the adult female rhino Rajeshwari in Dudhwa indicates that active predator–prey interactions are an integral component of managing a recovering rhino population within a tiger landscape with a high tiger population." But there is a limit to how much mortality a small or recovering population can absorb. "The rhino population in Dudhwa is limited and still aims for growth; as such, a high rate of predation will negatively impact the demography and population dynamics." Dudhwa's biggest lesson: release is only the beginning A rhino reintroduction cannot be treated as the finish line. "Dudhwa exemplifies a conservation story of return, resilience and the long road from reintroduction to rewilding," Sharma says. "The key lesson from Dudhwa is that reintroduction should be viewed as the beginning of population recovery; it teaches us to plan holistically to achieve a viable free-ranging population." A population of 50, 100 or 200 rhinos can remain vulnerable if it is isolated. For Sharma, resilience means several things happening at once. "The ability of the population to grow without continual human supplementation and connect naturally to be considered as a meta population including Nepal terai and communities to persist without perpetual intensive conflict will also be within the vision." That is why the 10 rhinos proposed for Dudhwa matter less as a number than as a beginning. The real test will come later, when rhinos are counted as members of a connected Terai population that can move, breed, survive, and coexist across a changing landscape.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News River Rights Movement in the UK Gains Ground as Communities Rally to Protect Local Waterways Reading Time: 3 minutes The river rights movement in the UK now connects around twenty grassroots groups working to give rivers legal standing. The river rights movement in the UK is growing steadily, uniting campaigners, co-ops, and community groups behind one shared goal. They want rivers to have real legal standing. Around twenty river groups now work together across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. The River Rights Network connects these local efforts under one umbrella. Instead of working in isolation, groups now share strategies, successes, and lessons learned. That collaboration has helped the river rights movement in the UK move faster than any single campaign could alone. Funding from an Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) Curiosity grant has helped the network expand. The grant supports four events, each hosted by a different member group, giving campaigners a direct chance to learn from each other. The first major event took place in Cambridge in September 2024. Friends of the River Cam hosted a workshop focused on rights. A second workshop followed in Sheffield in April 2025, hosted by OPUS Independents, exploring how rivers and their communities get a genuine say in decisions. Network members also joined the March for Clean Water in November 2024. Thousands turned out to call for healthier rivers nationwide. That visibility helps keep the river rights movement in the UK on the national agenda. Local campaigns make up the backbone of this effort. Groups like Love Our Ouse, Friends of the Medway, and Sacred Severn each focus on a specific waterway. Others, including Voices of Water and the Bioregional Learning Centre, bring creative approaches to river advocacy. Love Our Ouse offers one of the clearest examples of what the river rights movement in the UK can achieve. The group helped develop the first Charter of Rights for a UK river to gain formal council backing, with the River Ouse in Sussex officially recognized as a living entity by the Lewes District Council. That milestone shows local advocacy can lead to real institutional change. The river rights movement in the UK reached a milestone when Love Our Ouse helped secure Lewes District Council’s formal recognition of the River Ouse in Sussex as a living entity, making it the first UK river charter to gain official council backing and proving that local advocacy can drive real institutional change. Photo by Mike Bird on Pexels. The Ouse case also highlights why this work matters. Data from the river tracker Top of the Poops recorded sewage pollution there 63 times in 2023 alone, exposing the waterway to 442 hours of contamination across four monitoring sites. Supporters hope the charter will help hold polluters accountable. Josh Levene, who leads the network’s Rivers of Hope project, has spent over 25 years working with river communities worldwide. He directed Love Our Ouse before taking on this wider role. His experience now helps guide new communities through similar processes. Rivers of Hope is the network’s flagship initiative for scaling up this work nationally. The project runs workshops with communities, catchment partnerships, and local councils to help people reconnect with their local river and explore what a rights-based approach could look like. The project follows five clear steps. It raises awareness about what river rights mean in practice and showcases tools, such as river charters and nature guardian programs, that communities can adapt. It also works to reconnect people with rivers they may have grown distant from. From there, Rivers of Hope helps communities weigh their options. Every river faces different pressures, so no single solution fits all. Finally, the project strengthens the broader movement, since each new charter adds weight to the next community’s case. This model already has global precedent to draw from. Rivers in New Zealand, India, and Ecuador have received forms of legal personhood in recent years. Campaigners behind the river rights movement in the UK are adapting those ideas to fit British law and British rivers. The stakes remain significant nationwide. Many English rivers face pollution from sewage overflows, agricultural runoff, and aging infrastructure. Giving rivers a stronger legal voice could change how those long-standing problems finally get addressed. Nearly 20 rivers, from the Dart in Devon to the Tyne in the northeast, now have active local campaigns tied to the network. Some focus on legal recognition, while others prioritize education or council engagement. All share the belief that rivers deserve protection as living systems, not just resources. The success at the River Ouse has already inspired similar efforts elsewhere in England. New groups are welcome to join the river rights movement in the UK at any point. The network continues to grow as more communities decide their rivers are worth fighting for. What began as scattered local campaigns has become a coordinated national effort. Communities are learning from each other, sharing tools, and building a stronger case together. As more rivers gain formal recognition, the movement’s influence on UK water policy looks set to grow. The post River Rights Movement in the UK Gains Ground as Communities Rally to Protect Local Waterways appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αυτή η σύγχυση δεν τον εγκατέλειψε ποτέ, και όταν αργότερα ο παππούς του διαγνώστηκε με καρκίνο -- και ο Ζανγκ είδε την ίδια σύγχυση στο πρόσωπο της επτάχρονης αδερφής του -- έγινε ο σπόρος του…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Daniel Zhang was nine, he watched his grandmother lose her hair to chemotherapy and couldn't understand why medicine could look so much like harm. That confusion never left him, and when his grandfather was later diagnosed with cancer -- and Zhang saw the same bewilderment on his seven-year-old sister's face -- it became the seed of something purposeful. He and his classmate Zachary Tou, both 17, built *Tumor Tactics*, a Pok mon-inspired card game that teaches children cancer biology through the same mechanics they already love -- where, as Zhang explains, "chemotherapy can be a really powerful treatment, but you have to roll a die to determine how effective it is, and you might have to skip your next turn to recover from its side effects." What began as one boy trying to translate grief into language a child could hold has grown into a student-led nonprofit running workshops across San Diego schools, reaching kids from kindergarten through eighth grade. Perhaps most quietly remarkable is what happens at the end of each session: Zhang and Tou open the floor for discussion, and children -- unbidden -- begin sharing their own family stories, needing not just explanation, but the invitation to be heard.

Γνωστή για τη δημιουργία παραδοσιακών σχεδίων Μπενγκάλι Alpona έξω από τα κατώφλια της πόρτας, ξεκίνησε με μια απλή ιδέα: να εκπλήξει τους ανθρώπους και να φωτίσει τη μέρα τους. Αυτό που ξεκίνησε ως μια μικρή πρωτοβουλία έχει εξελιχθεί σε μια όμορφη αποστολή για τη διατήρηση της πολιτιστικής κληρονομιάς της Βεγγάλης…
items.descriptionOriginal: At 74, Ratnabali Ghosh wakes up at 5:30 AM to bring smiles to Kolkata’s streets, one Alpona at a time! Known for creating traditional Bengali Alpona designs outside doorsteps, she began with a simple idea: surprise people and brighten their day. What started as a small initiative has grown into a beautiful mission to preserve Bengal’s cultural heritage. From decorating dilapidated houses to bringing joy to elderly couples and slum residents, her art reminds us that beauty and kindness belong everywhere. Inspired by her grandmother and Rabindranath Tagore’s artistic legacy, Ratnabali hopes to revive a fading Bengali tradition and pass it on to future generations. Her story carries a powerful message: modernisation matters, but our cultural roots deserve to be cherished, too. Sometimes, preserving a tradition begins with one person, a little creativity and the desire to make someone smile. Do you think traditional Indian art deserves more space in our modern cities? items.descriptionOriginal: Growing vegetables and herbs on a balcony can be rewarding, but a healthy-looking plant does not always translate into a good harvest. Despite regular watering and adequate sunlight , tomatoes may yield fewer fruits than expected, herbs may struggle to grow, and vegetables may lack the flavour gardeners hoped for. The problem could lie in the conditions specific to the balcony. Dr Mayur Mandrah, an ex-Army major who shares gardening advice on Instagram as @plantwithmayur , has highlighted three common mistakes that can affect the growth of edible plants in containers. His advice focuses on understanding what plants need below the soil as well as the conditions in which they grow. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dr Mayur Mandrah, Ex Army Major (@plantwithmayur) 1. Choose the right soil for your pots Garden soil and potting mix serve different purposes. According to Mayur, using ordinary garden soil in containers can cause problems because it tends to compact over time. This reduces the air available to the roots, making it harder for plants to absorb the nutrients they need to grow. He recommends using a good-quality potting mix with adequate drainage instead. A suitable mix helps maintain airflow around the roots while allowing excess water to drain away. For balcony gardeners, choosing the right growing medium is an important first step towards healthier plants and a better harvest. 2. Give your plants enough room to grow The size of a pot matters beyond how well it fits into a balcony garden. A plant may appear healthy above the soil while its roots struggle for space in a shallow container. The gardener recommends providing tomatoes with at least 12 inches of soil depth and peppers with at least 10 inches. Even herbs such as basil can benefit from having sufficient room for their roots to develop. Before planting, check whether the container is deep enough for the crop you intend to grow. A pot that looks attractive may not necessarily offer the space the plant needs to survive. 3. Pay attention to your balcony's microclimate Balconies can expose plants to conditions that are different from those in a garden bed. Wind can dry out potting mix more quickly, while walls and floors absorb heat during the day and release it later. These changing conditions can place plants under stress and affect their growth and flavour. Mayur advises gardeners to spend time observing their balconies at different points throughout the day. Notice which areas receive direct sunlight, where the wind is strongest, and which spots become particularly hot. Based on these observations, move pots to locations that better suit their needs. A little attention to the conditions around the plants can help gardeners make better decisions about where to place them. Growing vegetables and herbs on a balcony can be rewarding, but a healthy-looking plant does not always translate into a good harvest. Photograph: (Ruff Day Vet + Pet Gym) Start with these three changes A productive balcony garden depends on more than regular watering and sunlight. The soil must support healthy roots, containers must provide enough depth, and plants need to be placed where they can cope with the surrounding conditions. By addressing these three factors, balcony gardeners can give their edible plants a better chance of growing well and producing a more satisfying harvest.

items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Peter McGraw, καθηγητή μάρκετινγκ και ψυχολογίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Colorado Boulder, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Τα σόλο ταξίδια αυξάνονται — και μια βιομηχανία…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Peter McGraw , a professor of marketing and psychology at the University of Colorado Boulder, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Solo travel is surging — and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving “solo travel” hit an all-time high this year, with queries for “women solo travel” reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton’s 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year, and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. The issue isn’t new. In 1992, marketing researchers identified the solo consumer as an underserved market . But as tourism researchers have documented , the accommodation sector treats double occupancy as the default unit of consumption, which often slaps a “single supplement” charge on customers when they travel without a partner. The industry essentially penalizes travelers for arriving without a second body to fill the other half of a room they aren’t using. The reason why so many hotels, cruise lines, and tour operators still base prices on double occupancy is that their costs — the room, the berth, the coach seat, the guide — don’t fall by half when the second person fails to materialize. But the supplement isn’t just a pricing convention. It’s the clearest signal the industry sends about who it built the product for. I’m a scholar who studies what I call the solo economy : how institutions and markets adapt, or fail to adapt, to the rise of single living. I’ve written before about how retail and restaurants still design for pairs. Travel is further along than most in recognizing this cultural shift. It’s also a useful case because the industry has started on the easy part of the problem but barely touched the rest. Demographics Matter, but Not the Way You’d Think The broader shift toward solo living is real. In 2025, 39.7 million Americans lived alone . That’s 29% of all households, up from 20% in 1975. Married couples, meanwhile, fell to 47% of households from 66% 50 years earlier. Those numbers alone don’t explain solo travel. Some of that decline went to people living alone; some went to unmarried couples, who are still a party of two on a booking page. Married people take trips alone. Single people travel with friends, siblings and parents, and plenty of them have logged serious hours as an extra wheel. Living alone and vacationing alone are different behaviors with different causes. What connects them is the erosion of a single assumption: that every adult arrives with a plus-one. That assumption is weakening at home, and it’s now encountering the booking page. Price Is the Easy Rung One response by the travel industry has been to shave the single supplement. For example, the tour operator Tauck announced this year that it’s waiving the single supplement on a class of its riverboat cabins across more than 250 European river cruise departures and reducing it by up to US$600 on 105 land departures. Another touring company has taken a more committed approach to adjusting its offerings: Aurora Expeditions sets aside 10 dedicated solo cabins on every sailing across its three ships, with no single supplement, through its 2026 and 2027 seasons. Then there’s Norwegian Cruise Line, which was early to the shift. In 2010, it introduced Studio staterooms aboard Norwegian Epic: small cabins designed for one passenger, sold at single-occupancy prices and arranged around a keycard-access Studio Lounge reserved for solo travelers. The trade-off is less private space, but at a price for one, with access to a room full of fellow travelers going it alone. Norwegian then expanded solo categories in 2024 from nine ships to its full 19-ship fleet. But on ships without Studios, much of the expansion was relabeling. Cruise Critic reported that standard double-occupancy rooms would likely be reclassified rather than retrofitted. And by Norwegian’s own account , the Studio Lounge is reserved for guests in Solo Studios — so the fleetwide solo categories come with the discount but not the room full of other solo travelers. That’s the difference between repricing and redesigning. The 2010 Studio was a purpose-built 100-square-foot (9 square-meter) cabin that cost Norwegian something to construct. The 2024 categories are, in many cases, the same rooms as before, with a new label and a discount. The solo traveler pays less than two people would, but it’s still more than half for a room sized and built for two. A cabin sold to one occupies the same space as a cabin sold to two, and the industry still counts berths. There’s a cleaner approach. Yotel sells a room type it calls Solo — 114 square feet (about 10 square meters) in New York City, maximum occupancy one, at the bottom of its price range. Nothing was subtracted to make it. It was built at that size, for that guest, and priced accordingly. That’s what designing for one looks like, and it’s rare enough that a tiny room counts as progress. alvarez—E+/Getty Images Many solo travelers seek control over their experiences and schedules, but they still seek a social component. Traveling Alone Doesn’t Mean Being Alone A common mistake in designing for solo travelers is assuming that solitude is the product. It isn’t. In the same 2026 data showing record interest in solo travel, Google found that searches for “travel groups” and “tour groups” also hit record highs . A Mastercard survey of more than 15,000 consumers across 11 countries found that 39% of international travelers had already taken a trip alone — and 7 in 10 international leisure travelers were interested in solo experiences built to connect them with like-minded people. The contradiction makes sense when you acknowledge that privacy and isolation are two different things. A person can want total control over where to go, when to eat, and when to return to the room — and still want company at dinner. The issue with double-occupancy pricing is that it assumes the customer brings their own company. But when only one person books, the operator has to address the pricing problem — whether or how to discount; and a product problem — how to supply a social component. Waiving a solo supplement solves the first issue, but it ignores the second. Norwegian understood this in 2010 by creating its lounge for solo travelers. The Pitch Is Easier When the Product Is for One For all these changes, travel advertising often still runs on couples: two glasses of wine, two lounge chairs, two silhouettes against a sunset. Sandals Resorts built an entire resort category around the premise. When solo travel does appear, it gets a different script. The traveler is adventurous, on a journey of self-discovery. AARP’s current solo-travel guide emphasizes personal growth and self-reliance. Even Norwegian closes its solo pitch by reassuring the reader that “you’re pretty good company.” The effect is to mark solo travel as exceptional at precisely the moment it stops being exceptional. Nobody reassures a couple that they will enjoy the balcony. Calling a solo traveler “brave” can be a compliment, but it can also reveal the assumption that traveling alone is abnormal, even when that’s changing. That all said, parts of the tourism industry have taken big steps over the past 15 years. But treating solo travelers as an audience rather than an accommodation is harder. It’s about selling them what they have already said they want: control over the trip, and access to other people, on their own terms. Marketing researchers named this opportunity in 1992. Thirty-four years later, the industry is still learning to build for one. Meanwhile, the solo traveler is standing at reception, holding a credit card, waiting for someone to design a room. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. A 300-square-meter (about 3,230-square-foot) noise barrier in Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, is being used to test passive greening: moss growing from natural moisture alone, no watering involved. The porous structure of moss may also help absorb sound, which makes the noise barrier a natural fit for the technology. A 260-square-meter (about 2,800-square-foot) social housing facade in Purmerend was one of the first practical applications. Traditional greening options were rejected there as too expensive and maintenance-heavy, and the project helped Respyre work out how bioreceptive facades are best designed and applied. In Haarlem, a 313-square-meter (about 3,370-square-foot) commercial renovation combined Mosscrete with insulation, aiming to both green the facade and improve thermal performance. Research published in June 2026 in the journal Science of the Total Environment found the effect is moisture-dependent: wet moss creates a cooling effect through evaporation, while dry moss can overheat in direct sunlight. In Amsterdam, the technology is being tested on bridge piers where graffiti has been a persistent problem. Moss-covered surfaces are less appealing as targets, and since the site has no irrigation, the project is also tracking how moss develops under ordinary conditions of rain, shade, and humidity. Designing for change Respyre is betting on a different idea of what building materials should do. Most are made to resist change, to stay gray and sealed for decades. Mosscrete is made for the opposite: it works best when moss gradually takes over. Urban greening helps manage stormwater and heat in dense cities, and there’s evidence it supports local biodiversity too. But a building slowly covered in moss doesn’t look like neglect. It looks like something is alive there. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.title: Η εκπληκτική ιστορία της κολοκύθας: από το αρχαίο βασικό μέχρι το εικονίδιο του φθινοπώρου
items.titleOriginal: The surprising history of pumpkins: from ancient staple to autumn icon
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Κολοκύθα lattes μπαχαρικών, φαναράκια jack-o'-hanterns και πίτες για την Ημέρα των Ευχαριστιών: οι κολοκύθες είναι οι ανεπίσημες μασκότ του φθινοπώρου. Αλλά πίσω από την εποχιακή τους γοητεία κρύβεται μια βαθύτερη, πιο περίπλοκη ιστορία που διασχίζει τη γλώσσα, την ιστορία, τη γεωργία και ακόμη και μια μικρή υβριστική κωμωδία. «Οι κολοκύθες είναι πιο δημοφιλείς από ποτέ», λέει η Cindy…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Pumpkin spice lattes, jack-o’-lanterns, and Thanksgiving pies : pumpkins are the unofficial mascots of fall. But behind their seasonal charm lies a deeper, more complicated story that winds through language, history, agriculture, and even a little insult comedy. “ Pumpkins are more popular than ever,” says Cindy Ott , associate professor of history at the University of Delaware and author of Pumpkin: The Curious History of an American Icon. But our obsession with this humble gourd, she notes, is tied less to flavor and more to a nostalgic longing for simpler, rural times. “People are buying these things, even pumpkin spice lattes, because of these attachments, these very old-fashioned ideas about reverence of the small family farm.” A name with roots that twist like a vine The word “pumpkin” has always been more conceptual than botanical. According to Logan Kistler , curator of archaeobotany at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, the term refers to squash varieties bred to resemble the round, orange gourds we associate with fall. “Pumpkin isn’t exactly a botanical group,” he explains. Linguistically, the word has had quite a journey. Fiona McPherson of the Oxford English Dictionary traces it from the Greek pepon to the French pompon , which eventually morphed into the English “ pompion ” in the 1500s. “Pumpkin,” as we know it today, first appeared in print in 1647, ironically in reference to the meager diet of early settlers. But while the word took a European path, the plant itself is deeply American. Indigenous peoples across North, Central, and South America cultivated early pumpkin ancestors, domesticating different types of Cucurbita as far back as 10,000 years ago in Mexico. “Pumpkins are part of this genus Cucurbita,” says Kistler, noting that they were farmed widely throughout the Americas long before colonists arrived. From insult to endearment Surprisingly, it didn’t take long for the word “pumpkin” to go from dietary staple to verbal jab. By the late 1600s, it was being used as an insult. “It really did not take long for it to develop this figurative use,” says McPherson. Pumpkin became a shorthand for someone who was conceited, dim-witted, or full of hot air. Cindy Ott adds that gender played a role in the insult’s direction. For women, pumpkin imagery was linked to the body and “natural urges,” seen as a lack of refinement. For men, it implied an empty head. “It’s been used for politicians for hundreds of years,” she notes. A symbol of imagined agrarian purity By the late 19th century, the pumpkin was undergoing a cultural rehabilitation. It shifted from insult to affection, and from staple crop to nostalgic icon. “So Americans move out of the country, into the city, but they like to imagine themselves farmers at heart, many of them,” Ott explains. As industrialization transformed the U.S., the pumpkin came to symbolize the pastoral life being left behind. In poetry, paintings, and festivals, it became a stand-in for tradition and a romanticized vision of national roots. Today, that symbolism is being put to work, literally. Pumpkins are once again supporting small farmers, not as dietary staples but as attractions. Ott calls them “agrarian wonderlands,” where farms market autumnal experiences that hinge on the iconic gourd. “The cool thing about the whole story,” Ott says, “is that these very romantic ideas and myths that a lot of Americans tell themselves about their origin stories are actually helping to rejuvenate the very thing it represents: a small family farm.” Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: Every couple argues . It might be about the dishes, the budget, raising kids, or dealing with the in-laws. Some fights are big, some are small. Most of the time, it blows over pretty fast. Disagreements are a natural part of sharing your life , your home, and your heart with another person. Occasionally, small misunderstandings quickly snowball into something larger . The kind of full-fledged, exhausting fight where nobody wins and both people walk away feeling hurt. Marriage and family therapists say there’s a surprisingly simple way to keep these disagreements from spiraling out of control. It’s called the partial concession. What is a partial concession? It’s exactly what it sounds like. You acknowledge the portion of the problem that you’re responsible for. You’re not conceding the whole argument, just your piece. It might sound something like “You’re right, I said I’d handle that, and I dropped the ball.” Or “I can see why what I said came across as dismissive.” At its core, a partial concession means stepping back and acknowledging the truth in what your partner says. That matters, even if you disagree with how your partner is framing the issue. You aren’t surrendering your whole argument. You’re just not pretending like you had nothing to do with it. Why it works First, it shows you’re actively listening. Your partner can tell you’ve actually heard and believed them, rather than just waiting for your turn to talk. The goal is to de-escalate and take oxygen away from the fire before emotions reach a point of no return. By validating your loved one’s points while holding space for your own, you transform a potential shouting match into a productive conversation. Once the pressure is reduced, it’s a lot easier to find a solution and move forward. The conversation can shift from “Whose fault is this?” to “What do we do now?” Research supports the effectiveness of a partial concession. In a study of 953 married or cohabiting couples, Baylor psychologist Keith Sanford found that when people feel blamed or criticized, they tend to want their partner to back off. That can mean admitting faults, showing respect, and being willing to compromise. Make it real, rather than just making a point A few tips make the difference between a real concession and a hollow one: Be specific. “Fine, I’m sorry you feel that way” doesn’t count. If you had committed to doing a task and forgot, admit your mistake. No one’s perfect, after all. Do it early. Don’t wait until you feel completely justified. You can release a lot of the steam from an argument by acknowledging your part sooner, rather than waiting until you feel you’ve said everything you want to get off your chest. Negotiate from a place of strength—being honest displays that strength. Don’t retreat entirely. You can concede a piece of an argument and still hold your ground on the rest. By acknowledging their valid points, you can turn a potential shouting match into a productive conversation. Relationships aren’t about keeping score or proving who is right. Sometimes, the smartest thing you can do is take a deep breath…and yield. Just a little bit. That way, you can build a sturdy bridge back to each other, where you wanted to be all along. The post Couples therapists say this simple move takes the heat out of almost any disagreement appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο ειδικός στο Charisma χρησιμοποιεί το «Ted Lasso» για να επεξηγήσει 6 στρατηγικές για τον χειρισμό της ασέβειας
items.titleOriginal: Charisma expert uses ‘Ted Lasso’ to illustrate 6 strategies for handling disrespect
items.description: Ο αριθμός των μαθημάτων ζωής που μπορεί κανείς να αντλήσει από τον Ted Lasso είναι αρκετά εντυπωσιακός, όπως μπορούν να επιβεβαιώσουν οι θαυμαστές. Η περίφημη σειρά που νιώθει καλά, γνωστή για την καρδιά και το χιούμορ της, προσφέρει μια τεράστια βοήθεια ψυχοσυναισθηματικής σοφίας τυλιγμένη σε ένα ταπεινό, λαϊκό πακέτο. Το δημοφιλές κανάλι YouTube Charisma on Demand έχει συγκεντρώσει και συσκευάσει μέρος αυτής της σοφίας σε ένα βίντεο…
items.descriptionOriginal: The number of life lessons one can glean from Ted Lasso is quite impressive, as fans can attest. The famously feel-good series, known for its heart and humor, offers a hefty helping of psycho-emotional wisdom wrapped in a humble, folksy package. The popular YouTube channel Charisma on Demand has compiled and packaged some of that wisdom in a video about how to handle disrespect. Most of us will, at some point, find ourselves on the receiving end of judgment, rudeness, passive-aggressive attacks, or other forms of disrespect. As Dr. Nina Ahuja writes in Psychology Today, disrespect can change us, affecting our willingness to speak up, our self-image, and our ability to recognize its impact over time. But with some conscious strategies, we can avoid letting disrespect derail us and even become “immune” to it. Charisma on Demand shared six ways to wisely handle disrespect, with examples from Ted Lasso (which you can watch in the video above): Remember disrespect isn’t about you Even though it can feel very personal, someone’s disrespect has nothing to do with you. “Sometimes it can be the other person’s insecurity or their fear, and sometimes it’s their need to feel superior,” the video states. “For many people, they’ve been using these defense mechanisms for so long that it’s simply just become a habit. Whatever the reason, it’s always coming from them, not you.” You aren’t responsible for the way someone else behaves, and what they do or say broadcasts something about them, not you. It’s easy to internalize anything that feels critical or negative toward us and start wondering what we need to change about ourselves. “Sometimes we become so convinced that we’re the ones to blame that we see disrespect where it wasn’t even intended,” the video points out. Assume positive intent “Sometimes it’s not obvious whether a comment is meant as an insult or if it’s just bad phrasing,” the video says. Either way, you can defuse a disrespectful statement by reacting as if the person had the best intentions. Ted’s character is a master at this. No matter what barbs other characters throw at him, he always responds as if their comments were neutral at worst. Relationship cheat code: Assume positive intent. That passive aggressive email? They were probably just rushed. Stinging feedback? They just want you to succeed. Don't assign sinister motives to innocent actions. Assuming the worst creates enemies. Assuming the best builds trust. — Dave Kline (@dklineii) December 2, 2025 However, there is a note of caution: “If insulting or passive-aggressive behavior persists, you can’t just keep assuming positive intent. If you keep pretending that you don’t see repeated disrespect, you end up being walked over. So assume positive intent once and then respond non-defensively.” People love to see a clapback, but as Charisma on Command points out, those kinds of zingers rarely work. Practice the art of non-defensive response The first step is simply to pause before responding. “Pausing for 5 to 7 seconds will give you a moment to breathe, which allows you to find the best response instead of just being reactive,” the video explains. “It’ll also force that person to sit with the comment they just made. And when they don’t get an immediate reaction from you, the silence can become very uncomfortable for them.” They may even walk back their comment after they’ve sat with it for a moment. Another non-defensive response is to go in the opposite direction and offer the person a compliment. “Now, this can sound counterintuitive, but complimenting someone who is disrespecting you can break that combative frame. It’s easy to fight with someone who is fighting back. It is much harder to fight with someone who is saying positive things about you.” Watch Ted do just that: Just make sure you find something genuinely complimentary to say, as forced praise can come across as either passive-aggressive or people-pleasing, which won’t help you. Set boundaries and enforce them Sometimes you need to draw a line and make sure someone doesn’t cross it without consequences. In fact, setting and keeping a boundary can help prevent a situation from escalating. “A strong boundary should be one clear sentence that focuses on what you are going to do if someone else persists or does something,” the video explains. “So, you might say, ‘If you keep making jokes about my appearance, I’m going to leave.’ Now, if the disrespect continues, there is no shame in walking away. And if you are repeatedly assuming positive intent, responding non-defensively, setting boundaries, and they’re still being disrespectful, the best thing that you can do is to remove yourself from that situation.” But always return to the first tip and remember: disrespect isn’t about you. If that’s true, what’s at the bottom of it? Get curious One of the greatest scenes in Ted Lasso is when Ted gives a little speech while playing darts with the show’s biggest antagonist, Rupert. He shares that the quote, “Be curious, not judgmental,” helped him realize every bully who’d ever underestimated him had lacked curiosity. Then he hit bullseyes on every shot, pointing out that Rupert hadn’t even asked if he’d played darts before challenging him to a contest. “Genuine curiosity is disarming,” the video points out. “Disrespectful people expect reaction or debate, not curiosity and connection. So, ask open questions. Try to understand their point of view, even if you don’t think you’ll agree with them…If you ask the right questions, you can uncover the source of their disrespect. Sometimes they’re lashing out simply because they’re having a bad day. Other times, there’s something deeper going on. So, once you’ve asked that open question, give them space to answer without interrupting.” Gaining a greater understanding of where they’re coming from can help you respond more to the person than to the behavior. Step in when someone else is being disrespected This last tip for dealing with disrespect is actually a way to gain respect. It’s one thing to handle disrespect when it’s aimed at you. However, if you’re witnessing someone else being disrespected, even someone disrespecting themselves, you need a more direct response. Even non-confrontational Ted stepped in when Rupert said something disrespectful to his ex-wife (and Ted’s boss and friend) at the bar. “Hey!” he interjected. “Better manners when I’m holding a dart. Please.” View this post on Instagram “This is what it looks like to be truly immune to disrespect,” the video says. “You’re not just unaffected by it. You’re strong enough to defend others from it, too. That is how you become the person that people genuinely respect.” Thank you, Ted Lasso and Charisma on Demand, for the valuable lessons. You can follow Charisma on Command for more tips like this. The post Charisma expert uses ‘Ted Lasso’ to illustrate 6 strategies for handling disrespect appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: We all want to live a long and healthy life. But as we enter our 60s and beyond, and a lifetime of choices and genetic luck begins to show, the issue becomes increasingly urgent. When it comes to longevity , our bodies give us many clues about how well they will age. The good news is that we can improve many risk factors, no matter our age. Healthcare expert shares good signs that someone over 60 will have longevity Neal Shah is a healthcare researcher, innovator, and advocate for health equity in aging populations. He’s also a wildly popular social media creator with nearly half a million followers on YouTube. He recently filmed a short video about the signs he sees that someone over 60 is in for a long, healthy life. 1. Walking speed “This is one of the most reliable predictors that doctors have to assess your health,” Shah says. “Multiple studies show that older adults who walk at a brisk, natural pace live significantly longer than slow walkers.” He says that our muscular health, heart health, and balance are reflected in our natural walking speed, which is what makes it such a powerful indicator. “If you can still walk with purpose, I think that’s a very good sign.” 2. Grip strength “How hard you can squeeze is a surprising window into your whole body’s strength,” Shah says, adding that poor grip strength is often associated with higher rates of heart disease and earlier death. Grip strength is easy to test and improve at home. Dead hangs, or hanging from a bar for as long as possible, are a great indicator—30 seconds for women and 60 seconds for men are great targets . With practice and repetition, anyone can improve their numbers and their overall strength and health. 3. Standing up from a seated position “Can you stand up from a seated position without using your hands to push off?” Shah asks. “This one simple move tests your leg strength and balance all at the same time.” Other, similar tests include standing up from sitting on the floor with minimal use of hands and knees. Why is balance so important for longevity? One big reason is that balance issues contribute to falls in older adults, and falls often result in injuries that can rob a person of their ability to independently care for themselves, as well as shorten their lifespan. Avoiding falls by maintaining good strength and balance is a major key to living a long and healthy life. 4. Overall balance The next sign underscores the need for balance by directly testing it. “Being able to stand on one leg for about 10 seconds is a strong marker of longevity. Research has linked the inability to do it with a higher risk of dying in the years that follow.” Shah reiterates that after age 65, falls become one of the biggest dangers for many adults. 5. Staying socially connected “People with strong friendships and regular connection live longer than people who are isolated.” It doesn’t mean it’s not okay to enjoy quiet and solitude, but avoiding loneliness is massively important for adults over 60. “Chronic loneliness is as damaging to your health as even smoking 15 cigarettes a day.” 6. Quantity of movement A lot of people—not just older adults—exercise for 30 or 60 minutes per day but remain sedentary for much of the rest of the time. Shah says what’s actually more important as we age is the amount of time we spend moving rather than the intensity. “The people who live the longest tend to move constantly in small ways. Things like gardening, standing up often, walking to the mailbox. It’s that steady all day movement that matters most.” You don’t need to be a triathlete to live a long and healthy life. In fact, gentler and more consistent movement may be the key. Shah adds that people over 60 shouldn’t panic if they don’t pass any of the above tests with flying colors. “Every single one of these things can be improved at any age,” he says. Depending on where you start, improvement might mean adding a gentle daily walk and gradually increasing your walking speed. It might mean practicing balancing on one leg or incorporating strength training to improve full-body power and conditioning. Or, it might mean filling your calendar with more time spent with family and friends. None of the items above are a death sentence for anyone, but together they paint an extremely accurate picture of overall health that we can use to live a longer and healthier life. The post Elder-care researcher reveals 6 powerful clues older adults will live a long life appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Since 2021, the International Dog Photography Awards have given professional and amateur photographers alike a platform to showcase their artistic talent , celebrate beloved dog breeds , and shine a light on those that are often misunderstood. For the 2026 awards, Katie Brockman won Dog Photographer of the Year for her image of a pit bull sporting a newspaper crown and collar. The crown’s headlines read positively, including “Pit Bull Saves Family From Fire” and “Pit bull therapy dog teaches lessons, allays fears.” Meanwhile, the collar carries more negative headlines, such as “A time-bomb on a leash?” and “Words ‘pit bull’ have sparked hysteria.” The image, aptly titled Loved and Hated , clearly conveys the “complicated relationship” between humans and pit bulls and other “bully breeds.” Loved and Hated , Katie Brockman “The collar and chain represent breed bans, restrictions, and other ways pit bulls are punished simply for existing, while the crown and gentle hand represent the advocates who support and love the breed. Meanwhile, the dogs themselves are caught in the middle between the two sides,” explained Brockman. Brockman met Caldwell, her pit bull model, while volunteering at a shelter. He had been overlooked by adopters and developed behavioral issues, lessening his chances of adoption even further. By then, however, Brockman had “fallen in love” with the sweet and stoic pittie. She even bought a house to adopt him. “Where I live, it’s nearly impossible to find rentals that allow bully breeds,” she noted. Brockman submitted to the Studio category, which focuses on controlled lighting and creative work produced inside a photography studio. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs Reading Time: 3 minutes How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs Commercial buildings waste about 30% of their energy, and that’s just an average, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. In practice, that means part of your utility bill is probably paying to heat empty rooms, cool unoccupied offices, light parking lots after everyone has gone home, or keep equipment running on an outdated schedule. While that’s a remarkably high number for energy waste, it’s surprisingly easy to lower it significantly. Often, you can start with low-cost fixes before investing in more sustainable and energy-efficient upgrades. All that is really needed is a fresh, honest look at how the building actually operates. Find Out Where Most of the Waste Goes Before replacing any equipment, look at your data: where does the building actually use energy? Review your utility bills, demand charges, operating schedules, and, where available, interval data from smart meters. Look specifically at peak demand times; staggered startup schedules can significantly reduce demand charges. Also compare energy use against occupancy and production schedules. If consumption barely changes between a busy Monday and an empty Sunday, something deserves investigation. An energy audit or retro-commissioning study can take this further. In plain terms, you are checking whether the building still operates the way its designers intended. Get Serious About Building Controls According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), high-performance control strategies can reduce annual HVAC energy use by 30% across a range of commercial building types. Of course, this doesn’t mean every building will cut its HVAC bill by that exact amount, but it shows why controls deserve more attention than they usually get. Look at temperature setbacks, occupancy schedules, ventilation rates, economizer operation, and simultaneous heating and cooling. A building automation system is only as useful as its programming. If the system has sophisticated controls but nobody checks whether they still match actual occupancy, you have an expensive computer making the wrong decisions. Upgrade Lighting and Control It LED retrofits remain one of the more straightforward commercial efficiency projects, particularly in buildings with old fluorescent or high-intensity fixtures. But swapping fixtures and calling the job finished misses half the opportunity. Add occupancy sensors where spaces sit empty for long periods. Use daylight controls near windows and skylights. Put exterior and parking-lot lighting on appropriate schedules rather than relying on someone to remember to flip a switch. This is also where electrical expertise matters. Whether you operate a warehouse in Texas, an office in Colorado, or need an Albuquerque electrical contractor for a New Mexico facility, look for a provider that can handle both the electrical work and efficiency side of the project. Look Beyond the Big Systems Some of the easiest savings are hidden in ordinary equipment. Plug loads can become a significant energy drain in efficient buildings, particularly where computers, kitchen equipment, vending machines, and other devices remain powered outside working hours. Smart power strips, automatic shutdown schedules, and better equipment procurement can help. This is a good reason to use submeters in larger facilities. Instead of seeing one enormous monthly electricity number, you can separate major loads and identify what changed. Use Maintenance as an Energy Strategy A dirty filter, poorly calibrated sensor, worn weatherstripping, or failing motor doesn’t just create a maintenance problem. It can make equipment work harder and longer. Build energy checks into preventive maintenance rather than waiting for an obvious failure. Inspect: HVAC controls and sensor calibration, Lighting and setback schedules, Equipment operating outside occupied hours, Door seals and building envelope air leaks, Unusual shifts or spikes in consumption. DOE research has found that properly tuned controls alone can produce substantial savings, partly because controls in existing buildings often drift away from their intended settings over time. Not every green upgrade deserves a blank check. Rank projects by expected energy savings, installation cost, maintenance savings, useful life, demand reduction, and available utility incentives. The post How Commercial Buildings Can Reduce Energy Use and Lower Operating Costs appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Kolkata's 74-year-old Ratnabali Ghosh aka "Alpona Didi" wakes at 5:30 AM everyday to draw alpona outside strangers' doors, just to make them smile. every day to draw traditional Bengali alpona outside strangers' doorsteps, just to make them smile. Inspired by her mother, Ratnabali believes art is about making people feel welcome, valued and less alone. Even as age and arthritis make her work harder, she refuses to give up. This Durga Puja, discover how Alpona Didi is keeping Bengal's fading folk art alive, one doorstep at a time. From residential buildings to shopfronts and restaurant entrances, her traditional alpona designs greet people as they step out in the morning. Her story is a reminder that traditions survive when someone chooses to carry them forward and that kindness matters, even when nobody is watching. Know someone who'd love this story?
