items.descriptionOriginal: At 12:54 am on 7 March 2024, a small wild cat approached a man-made pond in a forest patch near Goa's Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary. It stopped to drink, unaware that a camera trap beside the water was recording its movements. The camera captured five short video clips, which would soon become an exciting discovery for wildlife researchers Akshita Pungaliya and Atul Borker. The visitor was a mainland leopard cat ( Prionailurus bengalensis ), a shy, elusive wild cat that had never been photographically documented in Goa, according to the researchers' published findings. The sighting became the state's first reported photographic record of the species, with the findings published in the IUCN Species Survival Commission's Cat News in 2025. But the researchers hadn't set out looking for a leopard cat. Their project began with a much simpler concern. Every February, a freshwater stream running through this forest patch would dry up, leaving animals with fewer places to drink as the hotter months approached. Akshita and Atul wondered whether a small artificial pond could make water available to wildlife during those months. They decided to create one and use a camera trap to see what happened. What they recorded would help them understand the animals using this forest, including one that had rarely been documented in the region. When the forest ran out of water Akshita and Atul have long been interested in wildlife species that receive less attention than animals such as tigers and elephants. In 2023, the two researchers co-founded Vanasa Conservation Foundation to work towards protecting lesser-known wildlife. Their work brought them to a patch of private forest land bordering Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary, where a seasonal stream offered an opportunity to understand how animals cope with disappearing water sources. "We wanted to understand if creating an artificial water source in these forest patches would actually be used by animals," Akshita tells The Better India. "We've been monitoring activity across the year, but the original plan was to provide it in the drier months." Before building the pond, however, the team wanted to find a spot that animals were already likely to visit. They walked through the forest looking for small trails, fruit remains and disturbed leaf litter. These were clues that mammals regularly passed through certain parts of the landscape. "We looked at places where we could see smaller trails made by mammals, food lying around, signs that told us this is a walking path they use," Akshita explains. Using these signs, they chose a suitable location, dug a small pond, lined it and filled it with water. The artificial pond had a capacity of 40 litres. A camera trap placed nearby would help the team find out whether animals discovered the water and, more importantly, whether they returned. As the recordings began coming in, the researchers got their first answers. The mainland leopard cat is one of Asia's most widespread wild cats, found across parts of India, Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Japan and the Russian Far East. Photograph: (Camera Trapped) Birds, squirrels and leopards began visiting The camera soon captured birds arriving to drink, mongooses stopping by and squirrels moving across the frame. As monitoring continued, the researchers began seeing larger visitors too, including Indian gaur and leopards. Giant squirrels also appeared in the footage. Some animals came so close to the camera that it could barely capture their bodies. Akshita recalls moments when "you can barely see the hooves." For a team hoping to understand whether wildlife would use the pond, the variety of visitors was encouraging. But what caught Akshita's attention was how some animals appeared to be returning to the same spot. "If we keep it on across seasons in the year, you see them getting used to that spot," she says. "Earlier they may have found it by chance, but now they recognise it." The repeated visits suggested that some animals were becoming familiar with the water source. Meanwhile, the camera was helping the researchers observe wildlife that might otherwise pass through the forest unseen. Across 390 camera-trap nights, they documented visits by several species. Among those recordings were the five clips of the mainland leopard cat drinking from the pond on 7 March 2024. "My co-founder and I were just really excited to see that this happened," Akshita says. Their excitement came from knowing how difficult it could be to photograph a species like this, particularly in a region with so few previous records. A wild cat that Goa had never photographed The mainland leopard cat is actually one of Asia's most widespread wild cats. It is found across parts of India, Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Japan and the Russian Far East, and is listed as Least Concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Yet there are still gaps in our understanding of where these cats live in India. Most records come from the southern Western Ghats, the Himalayas and the Northeast. In the northern Western Ghats, photographic sightings have been particularly scarce, with only two previously documented in the wider region. Wildlife checklists had suggested that leopard cats could occur in Goa, but researchers lacked photographic evidence from the state. The footage from Akshita and Atul's pond helped fill that gap. Part of the challenge is the animal's behaviour. Leopard cats are small, shy, mostly active at night and often move through dense vegetation, making them difficult to observe. "This cat doesn't work the same way tigers or leopards do," Akshita explains. "It's small, elusive, shy, and mostly active at night." Researchers can sometimes recognise individual cats through their coat markings, but obtaining repeated camera-trap records across large forests takes considerable time and effort. And that effort needs funding, which can be difficult to secure for lesser-studied species. "Wildlife research highly depends on funding," Akshita says. "And funding often goes towards larger species or species in conflict with humans." As a result, smaller carnivores often receive less research attention, even though they perform important roles within forests. Leopard cats, for instance, feed on rodents and other small animals, helping regulate prey populations. Understanding their movements and habitats can help researchers learn more about how these forest ecosystems function. This is why even a single confirmed photographic record can be valuable. It tells scientists that a species is present in a particular landscape and gives them a starting point for further research. For Akshita, the Goa finding also shows what can emerge from a relatively small conservation experiment. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nature's Nest Goa (@natures_nest_goa) Could more forests benefit from this idea? Creating an artificial pond like the one used in the project costs approximately Rs 30,000 to Rs 40,000, Akshita estimates. A basic camera trap can cost between Rs 8,000 and Rs 10,000, while a higher-end model costs around Rs 25,000. "This is in general a very low-cost plan," she says. The pond can provide a water source during dry months, while the camera trap helps reveal which animals visit the surrounding area. Akshita says nature resorts in Karnataka have already begun discussing similar interventions. For privately owned properties bordering forests, carefully planned projects like these could offer a way to contribute to conservation while learning more about local wildlife. But they also require an understanding of how different animals might respond. For instance, if smaller animals begin using the pond, could larger predators follow? "It could," Akshita says. "And I'm very sure a lot of bigger cats do use these areas, and maybe nature resorts don't even know them yet." That possibility makes careful monitoring important. People living or working near forests may have little idea of the different species passing through their surroundings, especially at night. And as Akshita points out, learning about those animals doesn't always require creating a new water source. "If you want to know what's in your backyard," she says, "sometimes you don't even need a waterhole. Just set up camera traps near good forest habitat." Her team's experience in Goa offers an example of why that curiosity matters. They began by noticing a stream that dried up every February. They followed the paths animals had made, created a small pond and placed a camera beside it to see who would come. The footage revealed a variety of animals visiting the water, including a leopard cat that had never been photographically documented in Goa before. Five short video clips gave researchers a new wildlife record and drew attention to a small wild cat that remains poorly studied in this part of India. And it all began because two researchers noticed that the animals in a patch of forest might need somewhere to drink.

items.descriptionOriginal: "1 Plant, 100 Uses" explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. Sugarcane is a familiar sight across India's agricultural landscape. Its sweet juice is a popular summer drink; its stalks are crushed to make sugar and jaggery, and its leaves can be used as cattle fodder. But the plant's usefulness does not end when the juice has been extracted. India produced 454.61 million tonnes of sugarcane in 2024-25, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare's Agricultural Statistics at a Glance 2024-25. Beyond sugar production, the crop also supplies raw materials for industries that use its fibrous residue and other by-products. From generating electricity and making paper to producing compostable tableware and enriching agricultural soil, sugarcane offers several uses beyond the kitchen. Even the fibrous residue left after crushing the stalks can become a valuable raw material for industries. Research by Indian agricultural institutions highlights how different parts of the crop can be put to use. Here are ways this everyday plant finds a purpose well beyond the sugar bowl. 1. Sweeten everyday foods Sugar is the most familiar product made from sugarcane. Its juice is processed to extract sucrose, then crystallised into the sugar used in homes, restaurants, and food manufacturing. Sugarcane is a familiar sight across India's agricultural landscape. Photograph: (Saveur) The crop also supplies traditional Indian sweeteners such as gur (jaggery) and khandsari sugar. Jaggery is made by boiling concentrated sugarcane juice until it solidifies and is widely used in regional sweets, laddoos, halwas, and traditional preparations. The Government of India's One District One Product portal provides further information on sugarcane-based products such as jaggery and molasses. 2. Make a refreshing drink Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular street-side drink across India, particularly during summer. Vendors crush the stalks to extract the juice, often serving it with lemon, ginger, or mint. The juice can also be boiled down to make jaggery. In traditional production, the fibrous residue left after extraction may be burnt to provide heat for boiling the juice. This allows one part of the plant to help process another. 3. Create compostable tableware The fibrous residue left after extracting sugarcane juice is called bagasse. Its fibres can be processed into plates and other disposable tableware, offering an alternative to conventional plastic products. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research's Central Institute for Research on Cotton Technology has developed a technology to produce disposable paper plates using sugarcane bagasse and banana pseudostem fibres. According to ICAR's technology note on creating wealth from agricultural waste , a production unit could manufacture between 10,000 and 30,000 paper plates a day, depending on its size. The process uses compression moulding to turn the fibres into usable products. This provides sugarcane-processing industries another way to use the residue left behind after crushing the stalks. 4. Generate electricity Bagasse can also serve as fuel. Sugar mills burn this fibrous residue in boilers to produce steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity. The electricity helps meet a mill's own energy requirements, while facilities with suitable infrastructure can supply surplus power to the grid. According to a Press Information Bureau release from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy , sugar mills have used bagasse-based cogeneration plants to produce steam and electricity for their operations and generate additional power for sale. 5. Turn waste into paper Bagasse contains cellulose , a component of plant fibres used in paper manufacturing. After suitable processing, it can be converted into paper and other fibre-based products. The Institute of Wood Science and Technology, under the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education , explains how bagasse can be used to manufacture particle boards. It also identifies the material as a potential source of pulp for paper production. Its juice is processed to extract sucrose, then crystallised into the sugar used in homes, restaurants, and food manufacturing. Photograph: (Gardening Know How) Using this residue can create another source of raw material for industries that rely on plant fibres. 6. Feed farm animals Sugarcane can support livestock farming, too. The green tops and leaves left after harvesting can be used as dry fodder for cattle, particularly when conventional fodder is scarce. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research's study on sugarcane trash as fodder explains how the material can be chopped and mixed with green fodder and concentrate feed. Its nutritional limitations mean it should be used as part of a balanced ration rather than as a complete feed on its own. 7. Enrich agricultural soil Press mud, also known as filter cake, is a by-product separated during sugar juice clarification. It contains organic matter and plant nutrients that can be useful in agriculture. After appropriate treatment, it can be incorporated into compost and soil amendments, helping return organic matter to farmland . Its composition should be checked before application to make sure it is suitable for the intended use. This provides another route for putting sugar-industry residues to productive use instead of treating them solely as waste. 8. Make particle boards Sugarcane bagasse can be used to manufacture particle boards, which are made by processing plant fibres or particles and binding them into sheets. These boards can be used in certain furniture and interior applications. The Institute of Wood Science and Technology's research on bagasse particle boards describes the material's fibre content and its potential in board manufacturing. This application turns a residue from sugar production into a material that can serve the construction and furniture industries. Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular street-side drink across India. Photograph: (Juice at Home) One crop, many possibilities Sugarcane's value lies not just in its sweet juice but also in the many products that can be made from its different parts. Making better use of these materials can reduce waste and create additional value for sugar mills and farmers. The key is to choose suitable processing methods so that more of the crop can be used productively.

items.titleOriginal: Good News in History, October 18

items.descriptionOriginal: Ten years after a childhood bike crash, Rika Matsuda unfolded an origami crane a stranger who witnessed the crash had given her and found a message written inside -- a Japanese expression meaning "cherish the moment," or more fully, that we should treasure each encounter because it may never come again. The man had slipped the words in quietly, without drawing attention to them, letting them wait until she was ready. What the story reveals is something almost too simple to name: that a caring stranger's gentleness, offered in a few unhurried minutes at a water fountain, can fold itself into a life and stay there. "He didn't say anything," Matsuda recalled. "He just smiled and handed me the origami crane."

items.descriptionOriginal: You’ve finished your morning Nice News read but are still craving some uplifting, thought-provoking media — might we suggest turning to a podcast next? We’re big fans of the medium (so much so that we released a season of our own podcast last year!) and love how these audio shows can inform, inspire, and entertain during mundane moments of the day. We rounded up nine engaging shows that we think are worth a spot on your playlist, whether you’re doing the dishes, walking the dog, or just looking to unwind on the couch. No Such Thing As a Fish Prepare to laugh and be amazed. The recipient of the Heinz Oberhummer Award for Science Communication in 2019, No Such Thing As a Fish features researchers from the BBC’s comedy game show QI who spotlight a trove of hilarious and mind-boggling facts they’ve dug up over the previous week. The episodes are sure to leave you smiling after each listen. “It explains what the Second World War and carrots have to do with each other or how long you have to cook a space egg,” per a statement from the Oberhummer Awards. “And while you listen, laugh, and marvel for 40 minutes, you often don’t notice how much you’ve learned.” On Humans A favorite of Nice News Assistant Editor Rebekah Brandes, On Humans seeks to answer three questions: “Where do we come from? How did we get here? And what kinds of creatures are we?” In each episode, host Ilari Mäkelä interviews scholars primarily about our origins as humans, delving into specific topics like shamans , why we laugh , and the early days of farming . The show “always leaves me feeling smarter and more curious,” Rebekah said. Good Hang With Amy Poehler Amy Poehler isn’t trying to dole out advice or “make you better” — she’s simply looking for a good time. In Good Hang , which won the first-ever Golden Globe for best podcast earlier this year, Poehler interviews celebs and other “fun people” to provide a cozy, relaxed alternative to the plethora of self-improvement-focused media out there. Start with standout episodes featuring Jennifer Lawrence, Seth Meyers, and Tina Fey. Home Cooking Pals Samin Nosrat, author of Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat , and Hrishikesh Hirway, creator and host of the podcast Song Exploder , dished up cooking advice for amateurs with a side of friendly banter in Home Cooking , which ran from 2020-2025. A self-described perfectionist, Nosrat explained to Vogue in 2020 that the show centers a different mindset around cooking: “It’s about putting something out there to make people feel comforted and like they have technical support in the kitchen and some way to pass the time by hanging out with these funny, very dorky friends.” Unconditional With Maggie Lawson Animal lovers know there’s something special about the bonds they share with their pets — and this podcast celebrates exactly that. Hosted by Psych actor Maggie Lawson, the series explores the special connection celebrities like Henry Winkler and Janel Parrish have with their pets, and features interviews with animal experts about the “healing effects” of our furry friends. “Anyone who is obsessed with their pets will feel so seen by this podcast,” said Nice News Writer Marika Spitulski, adding, “I already want to be [Lawson’s] friend and hang out with her dog Linus.” Weirdly Helpful How can we take control of our “news diet”? And what’s considered proper handshaking etiquette in our modern age? These questions and more are answered in Weirdly Helpful , a series of bite-size episodes (each around 20 minutes or less) that spotlight guests who cover unexpected but intriguing ways to make life better. “Thanks for making me feel inspired while giving me concrete steps to evolve,” one reviewer wrote. Happier With Gretchen Rubin In 2024, we picked Gretchen Rubin’s brain about practical ways to lead a happier life — and in her award-winning podcast, the author and happiness researcher shares more strategies, ideas, and personal anecdotes to inspire you to live joyfully. Try one of her “A Little Happier” episodes for a quick fix; each lays out a lesson in five minutes or less. You can also check out her “Move Happier” series, intended to be paired with 26 minutes of movement as part of her Move 26 in ’26 challenge . The Allusionist If you’re a fan of NPR’s “Word of the Week” series, we bet you’ll love The Allusionist , which won smartest podcast at the 2018 British Podcast Awards. In each episode, host Helen Zaltzman dives into the intricacies of language, including the etymology and cultural significance of some of our most used words (and profanities), with a hefty dose of humor. Start with her April 13 episode “Hues” to learn why some of Merriam-Webster’s lexicographers took decades to define certain color names. Get Birding On HBO Max, you can catch Sean Bean ruling his corner of Westeros as the Stark family patriarch in Game of Thrones . On your podcast feed, though, he’s a soothing presence pointing out birds as they fly over his garden. The English actor took over as host for Season 4 of Get Birding , inviting ornithologists into his backyard and beyond to talk all things avian. The biweekly episodes, which you can also watch on YouTube, cover everything from why birdsong makes us feel good to why birds sing at daybreak . items.descriptionOriginal: What if retirement offered an opportunity to give something back to the natural world? In Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, two retired neighbors, John Rice and John Sessler, are doing just that, transforming their farmland into thriving habitats for wildlife. Working alongside Smithsonian conservation scientists, they've helped protect nearly 2,500 acres of private land, creating corridors where animals can move, find food, and flourish. Their days are spent removing invasive plants, restoring native wildflowers, and watching the landscape slowly come back to life. What began as a personal love of nature has become something much larger: a living legacy of conservation, nurtured through patience, dedication, and the simple joy of caring for the land.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 13-year-old has earned the distinction of being “America’s top young scientist” for 2026, taking first place in 3M’s prestigious Young Scientist Challenge. Raji Doshi, an eighth grader from Farmington, Connecticut, won the contest with an algae-based invention that could help save marine ecosystems. She and nine other finalists aged 11-14 created their prototypes over the summer, each of them working with a mentor to develop their ideas. Raji won the $25,000 grand prize after the challenge’s final events on Oct. 12 and 13, presenting a natural system that addresses ocean acidification by increasing alkalinity and removing carbon dioxide. Ocean acidification, which began during the industrial revolution, is primarily caused by the seawater absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The change in PH reduces the abundance of carbonate ions: essential structures that many marine lifeforms, like corals and crustaceans, need to build their shells and skeletons. “Raji’s project reminds us that when you’re passionate about something, you can use that interest to change the world,” her mentor, 3M product engineering specialist Deborah Isabelle, said in a press release . “She loves collecting seashells and was distressed that ocean acidification is starting to damage the seashells and the creatures that live inside them.” The contest also recognizes two runners-up, who each received a $1,000 cash prize. The three honorees, all girls, point to promising changes in the STEM arena, where women have historically been underrepresented. Seventh grader Aaisha Asif came in second place for her eco-friendly adhesive made from natural proteins; and ninth grader Sharvi Mahajan took third for her EEG-based device that tracks fatigue and predicts microsleep, alerting drivers and others in high-risk fields. Looking at the full lineup of finalists , it’s clear the future of science is bright. “The 3M Young Scientist Challenge highlights the incredible potential of young people to tackle real-world challenges through science,” said William Brown, 3M Chairman and CEO. “The talent and creativity displayed by this year’s finalists was exceptional, and we congratulate Raji on earning the title of America’s Top Young Scientist.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Reading Time: 5 minutes 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Spending all day in a truly comfortable bra is already a challenge. Tracking down one made from 100% organic cotton – with legitimate certification to prove it – is even harder. The market for comfortable 100% organic cotton bras has expanded, but quality is all over the place, and plenty of labels that claim “natural” can’t back that up with documentation. Why Organic Cotton Matters for Everyday Comfort Most people don’t realize how chemically loaded a conventional bra can be. Standard synthetics and treated cotton often carry azo dyes, formaldehyde finishes, and PFAS, substances pressing directly against skin for hours every day. The Center for Environmental Health detected BPA in sports bras from major mainstream brands at levels up to 40 times the established safe limit. Certified organic cotton changes that picture. GOTS certification (Global Organic Textile Standard) controls the entire supply chain from farm to finished garment, banning the synthetic pesticides and chemical finishes that standard cotton processing allows. For people with sensitive skin, eczema, or simply a preference for fewer synthetics, a GOTS-certified bra isn’t a luxury; it’s a practical choice. And comfort follows naturally. Organic cotton breathes well, wicks moisture without relying on synthetic coatings, and softens with wear rather than pilling or stiffening. The absence of harsh dyes also means less skin irritation over time. 1. Q for Quinn Q for Quinn is a small, family-owned Canadian brand founded in 2018 by Melita Cyril, who originally designed organic cotton socks for her son’s eczema before expanding into a full line of natural-fiber essentials for adults and children. The brand’s bra and bralette lineup covers several styles: a criss-cross bralette, a pointelle bra, a racerback sports bra, a full bust sports bra, and a shelf tank. Fabrics come in either 95% organic cotton with 5% elastane or 100% organic cotton. The fully cotton styles are biodegradable end-to-end, using natural rubber-cotton elastics and 100% organic cotton thread throughout; pricing starts between $52 and $64, and sizing runs XS through 3XL. Every applicable product carries GOTS certification through Ecocert Greenlife under license 256894. Product pages spell out each component – body fabric, elastic, thread, and closures – so nothing in the construction is hidden. Undergarments are made in certified facilities in Tirupur, India, and the brand excludes chlorine bleach, azo dyes, and formaldehyde finishes from its entire supply chain. Where it fits: Women with sensitive skin, those avoiding chemical exposure during workouts, and shoppers who want full material transparency in a bra, particularly for low-to-medium impact activities like yoga, Pilates, and walking. 2. Roaman’s Roaman’s is a plus-size fashion retailer with roots stretching back decades, now operating as part of FullBeauty Brands and headquartered in Indianapolis. The brand focuses exclusively on sizes 12W through 44W, it doesn’t start from a smaller size and grade up, which makes it genuinely purpose-built for plus-size shoppers rather than an afterthought extension of a standard range. The catalog spans a wide range of women’s clothing, intimates, swimwear, sleepwear, tops, bottoms, and shoes. With over 100 years in women’s fashion, the brand positions itself as an industry leader and pushes fashion-forward designs at prices that don’t require a big budget. Shopping options include the website, a printed catalog, and a store credit card. Roaman’s clothing was used to dress cast members on TLC’s 1,000 lb Sisters , a placement that put the brand in front of its core audience. Customer support runs through phone and email, and the website offers account management, order tracking, and a rewards program. Where it fits: Plus-size shoppers looking for a wide selection of intimates and clothing in one place, with consistent sizing across categories. Worth checking: Roaman’s is a general plus-size fashion retailer. Shoppers seeking certified organic cotton bras should confirm material details before purchasing, as the brand doesn’t position itself around organic certification. 3. Siella Siella is a Canadian lingerie brand launched in 2020 out of Montreal, backed by Chateau Bodywear, a family business with over 75 years of experience manufacturing underwear and lingerie, founded in 1945. That manufacturing depth gives Siella a level of vertical control that newer brands rarely have. The line focuses on wireless bras, underwear, and loungewear, with a stated emphasis on comfort, support, and a second-skin fit. Siella describes its approach as designed by women, blending modern femininity with everyday comfort. Prices range from approximately $25 to $105 USD, with bundle discounts of up to 20% available. Free shipping kicks in on orders over $95. U.S. customer service operates on EST timezone at +1 800-665-0589. The brand emphasizes organic cotton options and benefits from its parent company’s manufacturing infrastructure, which supports tighter control than outsourced production typically allows. Siella has been featured in Diary of a Toronto Girl’s roundup of top lingerie brands. Where it fits: Shoppers who want wireless bras that prioritize everyday comfort and are open to a Canadian brand with a long manufacturing history behind it. Worth checking: Organic cotton certification details aren’t publicly disclosed the same way as some competitors, so shoppers should confirm certification before purchase if that’s a deciding factor. 4. Bestform Bestforms, Inc. is a company founded in 1985 and headquartered in Camarillo, California, with 51 to 200 employees. The company operates as a B2B manufacturer in the business forms and print industry, producing patented membership card products, integrated labels, variable barcoding, unit set forms, continuous forms, and custom labels. Bestforms describes its model as “trade only,” meaning it works through intermediaries rather than direct-to-consumer channels. The company’s tagline is “BestCards, Labels and Digital Solutions, Forms,” and its track record centers on responsive development for commercial printing needs. Bestforms does not appear to operate as a lingerie or apparel retailer. No bra products, organic cotton garments, or related consumer goods appear in the company’s product lineup. Where it fits: Business clients in need of commercial printing, label manufacturing, or custom card production, not a category match for consumers shopping for organic cotton bras. Worth checking: Shoppers searching for lingerie under this name should confirm they’ve reached the correct brand, as the bestform.com domain belongs to a commercial printing manufacturer, not an apparel company. 5. AmpleBosom AmpleBosom is a UK-based online and mail-order retailer founded in 1999 by Sally Robinson, operating from a family-run farm in Old Byland, North Yorkshire. The company specializes in bras, lingerie, swimwear, nightwear, and clothing, with a size range that runs from 28 to 58 in AA through N cups, one of the widest ranges available anywhere in the market. AmpleBosom doesn’t manufacture its own products; instead, it stocks bras and lingerie from established names including Empreinte, Elomi, and Fantasie. The team is estimated at 25 to 100 employees, and the business has stayed independent since it launched. It earned early recognition when the BBC series Inside Dot Coms featured it in 2000, notable for an e-commerce model that was well ahead of the mainstream at the time. Expert bra fitting advice is offered both in-person and virtually. Payment is accepted online, by mail, or by phone; in-store payment isn’t an option. Pricing varies by brand and item, with promotions available throughout the year. Where it fits: Shoppers who need larger or harder-to-find cup sizes and want access to multiple specialty lingerie brands in one place, with expert fitting support available. Worth checking: AmpleBosom is a UK retailer; U.S. shoppers should factor in international shipping costs and delivery times, and should verify whether specific organic cotton options are available among its current brand selection. Bottom Line Brands in the comfortable 100% organic cotton bra space span a surprisingly wide range – certified organic specialists, plus-size fashion retailers, and, in at least one case, a commercial printer that has no business appearing on this list. For shoppers who prioritize verified certification, full material transparency, and construction that’s genuinely gentle on sensitive skin, the real options thin out fast. Roaman’s and Siella both serve comfort-focused buyers but from different angles: Roaman’s through extended plus sizing, Siella through wireless everyday styles. AmpleBosom suits anyone needing an unusually wide cup range paired with professional fitting guidance. Know what matters most to you – certification, sizing, support level, or country of origin, and the right choice gets a lot clearer. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable Reading Time: 3 minutes How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable The lights flicker during a storm, and you suddenly notice the grid you rarely think about. More of your power now comes from the sun and wind, which don’t follow a schedule. Clean energy can remain steady as the weather shifts because modern grid upgrades help balance supply and demand and ensure reliability behind the scenes. What Is a Smart Grid? A smart grid is an electrical network that uses digital technology to monitor and manage power from the source to the home. It sits at the heart of grid modernization, which involves upgrading the physical equipment and digital tools that generate, move and manage electricity. Older grids relied on one-way communication, but a smart grid lets utilities and customers share information in both directions. The most visible piece is the smart meter. In 2022, utilities in the United States had about 119 million smart meter installations , or roughly 72% of all electric meters. Advanced versions have built-in two-way communication, so they can record and send data instantly. A smart grid relies on several connected parts working together: Smart meters: These devices track your energy use and share it with your utility. Sensors: Devices along power lines and equipment can flag problems before they spread. Automated switches: These switches can reroute power around a fault without waiting for a crew. Energy storage: Batteries save extra power , such as midday solar, for use when demand rises. Two-way communication: This link lets utilities and customers share data and respond to each other quickly. Why Does the Traditional Grid Struggle With Clean Energy? The grid that powers your home took shape in a very different energy world. Large, steady power plants sent electricity to homes long before rooftop solar panels or wind farms existed, and the equipment reflects that history. Today, over 70% of the power grid is over 25 years old. Variable solar and wind, plus growing demand, strain equipment with limited ability to see or adjust to changes in real time. Engineering and utility consulting firms help power companies plan upgrades to infrastructure, sensors and smart meters. Each improvement can give operators a clearer view of the system, enabling them to respond to changing conditions sooner and keep clean power flowing. That approach can turn an older network into a smart grid built for clean energy. How Can Upgraded Grids Balance Wind and Solar Power? Wind and utility-scale solar generated 17% of U.S. electricity in 2025, up from under 1% in 2005. However, wind and solar only produce power when the wind blows or the sun shines, unlike power plants that can ramp up on demand. Modern grids tackle the gap between when clean power is available and when you need it. Batteries can store surplus solar power for evening use, and smart controls can automatically adjust the grid as supply rises and falls. Forecasting can help operators predict wind and solar output in advance and prepare accordingly. Demand response programs can also encourage you to shift energy use to times when clean power is plentiful, easing pressure on the grid during peak hours. These tools may help wind and solar become a steadier part of your power supply. Why Does Extreme Weather Raise the Stakes for Reliability? Severe storms, heat and winter weather can all disrupt steady power. From 2000 to 2023, 80% of major U.S. outages were weather-related, with the latest decade seeing about twice as many as the first. A modernized grid can help keep your community’s power on when conditions turn rough. Sensors can quickly detect damage, and automated switches may isolate the damaged section so the outage affects fewer neighborhoods. Self-healing systems, which detect faults and automatically reroute electricity, can keep more homes connected. Microgrids, which are small, local networks that can operate independently, may also help restore power faster. Together, these tools can shorten the time you spend in the dark and make clean energy feel dependable even during difficult weather. What Could a Smart Grid Change in Your Daily Life? Smart grid upgrades can make clean energy more useful in daily life by changing how power moves to and from your home: Rooftop solar: A two-way grid can make it easier to send extra power from your panels back to your community. Time-of-use pricing: Some utilities offer lower rates during off-peak hours, which rewards flexible habits. Electric vehicle charging: Smart charging can schedule your car to charge during off-peak hours. Quicker repairs: Better monitoring may help crews find and fix problems faster. What Can You Do to Support Steady Clean Power? Clean energy is only as reliable as the grid that carries it. Grid modernization works quietly in the background to keep clean power steady in your home, from the smart meter on your house to the upgrades down the street. A good next step is checking what your own utility offers, such as smart meter data, time-of-use plans or solar programs. Small choices like these can help a more dependable, cleaner grid take shape, and you can find the options are closer than you think. The post How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems Reading Time: 4 minutes How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems Readers of this site tend to think in systems. A beaver dam that restores a creek, a wildlife crossing that saves panthers, a court that grants fish legal standing, these stories share a common thread: small, deliberate interventions ripple outward into healthier ecosystems. Pest control rarely gets discussed in that same frame, but it belongs there. Every spray, bait, or barrier a homeowner chooses either supports or undermines the insects, birds, and soil organisms that keep a neighborhood’s ecology functioning. That matters more than most people realize, because household pest management sits at the intersection of two things this audience cares about deeply: protecting pollinators and other wildlife, and making smart use of limited resources. The choices homeowners make about ants, termites, or rodents do not stay contained to a single yard. Chemicals drift, water carries residue, and beneficial insects do not distinguish between a target pest and a pollinator caught in the same treatment zone. In fast-growing communities around San Antonio, this tension shows up constantly as new development pushes into former ranchland and native habitat. Homeowners in that region increasingly ask pest professionals to treat infestations without collateral damage to the monarchs, native bees, and birds that still move through these corridors. Companies like EcoForce Pest Management , which serves the Cibolo, Texas area, reflect a broader shift in the industry toward targeted, lower-impact treatment methods that still get rid of pests without broadcasting pesticide across an entire property. Why Pest Control Choices Ripple Through Local Ecosystems Pollinators are not a side issue in this conversation, they are central to it. Insect pollinators add more than fifteen billion dollars in crop value annually in the United States, which means any pest control practice that harms bees, butterflies, or other pollinating insects carries a real economic cost well beyond the yard where it happens. Routine, calendar-based spraying, the kind that treats a property on a fixed schedule regardless of actual pest pressure, increases the odds of harming these beneficial insects compared to treatment that responds to an actual, identified problem. This is why the distinction between reactive, blanket pesticide use and targeted treatment matters so much ecologically. A homeowner who sprays broadly “just in case” is making a bet that trades short-term convenience for long-term harm to the insects and soil life that keep local food webs intact. A homeowner who waits for evidence of an actual infestation, then treats only the affected area, protects far more of the surrounding ecosystem while still solving the immediate problem. What Actually Drives the Cost of Pest Management Cost in pest control is rarely about the price of a single treatment, it is about how often treatment has to happen and how much damage accumulates before anyone intervenes. A termite colony left undetected for a year can cost thousands of dollars in structural repair, while the inspection that would have caught it early costs a fraction of that. Rodents chewing through wiring create fire risk and expensive repairs that dwarf the cost of sealing an entry point before they ever got inside. According to EPA , integrated pest management relies on monitoring, pest-identification thresholds, and preventive habitat changes, reserving chemical treatment as a targeted last resort rather than a routine first response. That framework is not just ecologically sound, it is financially sound too, because prevention and early detection cost less than remediation almost every time. The expensive scenarios are always the ones where a problem went unnoticed long enough to cause structural or health damage, not the ones where someone paid for a seasonal inspection. Where Eco-Friendly Methods Pay Off Over Time Eco-friendly pest control is sometimes assumed to be the pricier, more delicate option, but the opposite is often true over a multi-year horizon. Sealing cracks, managing moisture, and removing food sources reduces the pest pressure that would otherwise require repeat chemical treatments. Fewer treatments mean lower cumulative cost, and they mean less pesticide entering soil and groundwater where it can affect everything from earthworms to the birds that eat them. The table below lays out some of the real tradeoffs between reactive, chemical-heavy pest control and a more preventive, ecologically minded approach, using figures drawn from EPA guidance on integrated pest management. Factor Reactive, broadcast treatment Preventive, IPM-based approach Pollinator risk Higher, due to non-targeted exposure Lower, treatment is targeted to confirmed pests Core strategy Calendar-based spraying regardless of need Monitoring and thresholds before any chemical use Economic value protected Not factored into treatment decisions Helps preserve pollinators tied to $15B+ in annual crop value Lowest-cost prevention step Rarely prioritized Sealing entry points, moisture control, sanitation What this comparison shows is that the cheapest long-term option and the most ecologically responsible option tend to converge. A property that invests in sealing, drainage correction, and regular monitoring spends less over five years than one that relies on repeated broad-spectrum treatments, even though the upfront preventive work can look like an added expense in year one. Smart Places to Economize Without Compromising Protection Homeowners who want to save money without cutting corners ecologically should focus their budget on the structural fixes that prevent infestations in the first place, since these are the cheapest interventions with the longest payoff. Sealing foundation gaps, repairing damaged screens, and fixing leaky pipes that create standing water all cost far less than a single severe infestation treatment, and they address the root conditions that attract pests to begin with. These are also the steps least likely to involve any chemical exposure at all, which makes them a win on both the cost and ecological fronts. Where spending does make sense is in professional inspection and identification, because misdiagnosing a pest problem leads to wasted treatments and wasted money. A targeted response to a correctly identified pest, applied only where needed, almost always costs less over time than a generic, whole-property treatment applied out of uncertainty. For readers who care about the pollinators, soil organisms, and backyard wildlife that this site regularly celebrates, that targeted approach is also the one that does the least collateral damage to the ecosystem right outside the door. The post How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Arielle: Yeah, it’s been really weird here in the Netherlands as well. I would not complain about that, but it’s just, it’s a bit hard to get into the seasonal rhythm… I don’t know if our listeners and fellow Optimists are feeling similarly, but I know that I’m just feeling a bit weird. Other than that, nothing to report on my end. Karissa: Yeah. I feel similarly. I guess I’m enjoying a little bit of stillness between the busy summer months and the festive season. We’re gonna go full force into the holidays here, and then this year will be over, so um- Arielle: Yeah. It definitely went by quickly, but there’s still a lot of positive news out there to share before the end of the year. And if you want all of those positive solutions straight to your inbox, then you should consider signing up for our daily or weekly newsletter. You can do that on our website, or the link is in the show notes. Karissa: And if you want these solutions and more on your social media feeds, we’re @optimistdaily on everything except X, where we’re @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: You can also reach me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We would love to get any suggestions, comments, questions, feedback, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Before we go any further, we’d love to thank our Optimist Daily Emissaries who financially support us. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is in the show notes. If financially supporting us isn’t in your budget right now, we thank our Optimists who share these solutions and follow us on socials. Arielle: Yeah, there are a lot of free ways to support us, and we appreciate everyone who does that. Karissa: And without further ado, Arielle, I think we should dive into this week’s new solutions. Australia’s renewable energy record Karissa: The first one that we had to share this week is “Australia sets a new renewable energy record, with rooftop solar leading the way”. So Australia just hit a new record. Solar- and wind-powered 80% of the entire national grid on a single Saturday. And the wild part about that is that more than half of that came not from massive solar farms, but from panels on people’s rooftops. For about 30 minutes, 4.3 million rooftop solar installations collectively carried more than half of the country’s total power load. The researcher who tracks this called it record season. Conditions were so good, he expects these records to get broken again within weeks. These individual homeowners, and not, like, utility companies, drove a national record, and that’s exciting all in itself. Arielle: Yeah, it really drives home the point that the energy transition doesn’t have to center around big infrastructure. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: It’s a reminder that, yeah, if there’s small-scale adoption, then that can really add up quickly. Karissa: Absolutely. And with Australia having an 82% renewable target for 2030, this kind of milestone is expected to become routine. So that is optimistic indeed. Performance anxiety & sport psychology Karissa: The next solution is titled “”How to quiet performance anxiety, according to sport psychology””. A sport psychologist who works with NFL teams and Olympic athletes has a pretty counterintuitive take on confidence. You don’t wait until you feel it, you act your way into it first, fake it till you make it, and the feeling follows. So she has a whole toolkit for doing this in the middle of a high-pressure moment, and the technique that an NFL receiver used after a playoff fumble is one of them. I didn’t know about this technique, but it’s called the learn, burn, return method, which is a three-step process for recovering mid-performance from a mistake. Learn one thing from it, use a physical gesture to signal moving on. For example, the Vikings receiver Adam Thielen made the toilet flush gesture famous in a 2020 playoff game, where he’s just kind of pretending to flush the toilet and get rid of that mistake, which is a fun thing. And then reset it all with a certain phrase. The performance anxiety conversation used to live almost entirely in sports, but I mean, now it’s everywhere, whether it’s in job interviews, presentations, creative work, even dating. So I think it’s important to expand upon this concept. But yeah, there’s a lot of great tips in this article from Cindra Kamphoff, who is a PhD in sport and performance psychology, and she gives a lot of great tips here, including writing powerful phrases before a high-stakes moment, which I really liked that one. So go check it out if you want some more pointers. Coral shade experiment Karissa: The next solution is “”How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave””. Scientists in Florida just published results from an experiment where they literally put little floating umbrellas over coral to protect them from the heat, and it worked. But the lead researcher was pretty blunt. This is triage, not a total solution for coral bleaching. So I loved the images here in this solution, because it really had like… The um- umbrella is kind of a… It, it’s not… I at first pictured an umbrella, like our pop-up umbrella, and I thought that was kind of a cute image, but it’s kind of just a floating, like Arielle: Like a shade, Karissa: basically Shade, yeah. Like a, just a little piece of, um- Arielle: Yeah, like a tarp … Karissa: yeah, a tarp. That’s a great way to explain it. The shaded brain coral started recovering color after these umbrellas were put in, and the unprotected ones kept bleaching through the hottest part of the season. Coral bleaching events used to happen about once a decade, but now they’re happening every five to six years, and reefs don’t have enough time to recover between them. By March 2025, 84% of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures high enough to cause bleaching. The researcher’s quote in this was so honest, that shading is not a cure-all. This is a solution that is kind of just buying time for the bigger problem. Arielle: Yeah. It’s important to address the root problems, but yeah, if we need more time, which we definitely do, then why not? Karissa: Absolutely. Did you know that coral reefs cover less than 0.2% of the ocean floor, but shelter a quarter of all marine species? So that’s a pretty wild ratio, and we gotta protect them, just like we need to protect the rest of our beautiful planet as well. Skincare mistakes Karissa: The next solution is “”The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine””. Five dermatologists were asked what bad skin habits they most want patients to break, and the answer keeps coming back to the same thing. Most of us are overdoing it when it comes to our skin care routine. And there’s also a pimple popping rule in here that I think a lot of people will appreciate, and I’ll start with that one. It’s the one good squeeze rule for pimples. It’s okay to pop a pimple, but if it doesn’t come out on the first try, stop, because continuing just pushes bacteria deeper and can cause those dark spots that stick around for months. I admit if it has a white head, then I have to pop it. But usually, of course, that comes out with the one good squeeze, and it… I do think it’s, it’s very, um, satisfying, so. Arielle: Yeah. No, I’m so guilty of this. I love popping pimples. Karissa: Me too. Arielle: Um, and I will keep going at it, and I have had that, like, hyperpigmentation thing happen. Mm-hmm. And it’s just not cute. Yeah. And I, I have to abide by this. You know what’s really helped me, though? Those pimple patches. So- Karissa: Yeah, I was gonna say the same thing … Arielle: first of all, they’re fun, so you can have, like, a little purple star or whatever on your face instead of a- Yeah … a bright red glaring pimple. Um, but I do it less for, like, the… Well, of course I, I do it so that the pimple will heal, but it’s more so that my fingers just don’t get on it. Because if I see it- Yeah … then I just wanna squeeze it. Karissa: I resonated with the point that skin care has developed a trend cycle that rivals fast fashion. There’s new ingredients, new products every week, and TikTok routines that keep expanding what we’re, you know, supposed to do. So dermatologists really emphasize that sticking with simple is oftentimes better. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and just what works for your skin. Because everyone’s skin is different, and you can’t just be chasing the trends all the time if it doesn’t work for your specific type of skin. So if you have a routine that works for you, then just stick to that. Don’t get, like, you know, uh, distracted by the shiny new serum. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Exactly. Flu shot timing Karissa: Next solution is “”Why October is the best time to get your flu shot this year””. Flu is already showing up in emergency rooms across the West, and the numbers are running about seven times higher than the same week last year. Experts are saying October is the window to get vaccinated, and there’s actually a new mRNA flu vaccine in the mix for the first time, which is a really great breakthrough. So yeah, seven times higher than this time last year is pretty rough. It’s in Western states now, but it’s expected to spread east. And the flu vaccine’s effectiveness data is pretty interesting. 29 to 56% effective against of cases that send people to the doctor, but better against severe illness. The framing here with vaccines in general is to remember it’s keeping you out of the hospital, and keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery, which is a quote from the article. About the mRNA flu vaccine, you might recall this term being used for, uh, the COVID vaccine, and it’s now being applied to the flu vaccine for adults 50 and older this season, and it’s supposed to be more effective. Arielle: There was a, a number in this article that kind of broke my heart. It said that last year there were at least 195 child deaths from flu-related causes, and preventing such high numbers could be as simple as just getting vaccinated against the flu. So yeah, and I don’t mean to fearmonger, but it definitely struck a chord with me when I read it. Karissa: Yeah. Tens of thousands of Americans die of flu each season, and that tends to surprise people. I feel like flu deaths are chronically under-discussed. So of course, yeah, like you mentioned, Arielle, not to fearmonger, but get that flu vaccine, and it’s a good time to get it now. Octopus nursery Arielle: Well, on that note, we’re going to bring it to some lighter topics, let’s say. Uh, the first solution that I’m going to share with everyone is titled “Scientists discovered the world’s largest octopus nursery off the California coast”. Scientists were studying one of the most closely monitored stretches of ocean in the world, and somehow missed 20,000 octopuses just hanging out on the sea floor. Turns out there’s a field of hydrothermal springs down there that’s functioning as the world’s largest known octopus nursery, and researchers only found it in 2018. So these hydrothermal springs keep the water warm enough to cut the octopuses’ egg-brooding time from years down to about 1.8 years, which still sounds like a l- a long time to me. Yeah. But if it’s, if it’s cutting more years off of it, then that’s great. And this is why so many octopuses congregate there specifically. The octopuses build their dens from whatever they find on the sea floor, including human objects that have drifted down to the deep sea. This went undetected until 2018 in well-studied water, which raises the question of how many other gatherings like this exist in unmapped thermal fields elsewhere. There’s been growing public fascination, I think, with octopus intelligence and behavior in recent years, and this story lands right in that conversation. And yeah, I, I think I remember when My Octopus Teacher came out, and I think that was kind of when everybody was like, “Oh my gosh, octopuses are actually so, so smart and so cool.” Um, have you seen it, Karissa? Karissa: No, I haven’t, but now I wanna go watch it because I… this solution really, uh, stood out to me this week and I love it, so I’m really interested in learning some more. Arielle: Yeah, this week we have such cute ocean stories, like picturing little corals under their umbrellas and, like a whole bunch of octopuses chilling out. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Making babies. So… Karissa: Yeah, fun stuff. Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers Arielle: The next solution is titled “Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters”. A Japanese disaster scientist had an idea 20 years ago while studying earthquakes in Indonesia. What if the country’s mosque loudspeakers, already everywhere and already maintained daily, could double as earthquake warning systems? That pilot is now underway, and the drop-and-cover finding buried in the story is just as interesting. And if you don’t know what I mean by that, just wait. I will get to it. So Indonesia might have only five to 10 seconds of warning before an earthquake hits, and yeah, the mosque loudspeakers tested five times a day by local communities are more reliable than phone networks that can fail the moment the ground starts shaking. What I mean when I say that the mosque loudspeakers are tested five times a day is that, um, the call to prayer happens five times a day, so they definitely know that the speakers are working because the call to prayer is happening. And the drop-and-cover thing that I mentioned earlier is the standard international advice for when there’s an earthquake. You’re supposed to drop low and cover, like get under a table or something. But this advice was meant for places with well-constructed buildings, and in Indonesia, where homes are often unreinforced masonry, the people who survived earthquakes in the past actually ran outside. You know, there is growing conversation in disaster preparedness about community-maintained infrastructure versus centralized government systems, and this is a real case study for why local trust really matters. Indonesia and Japan are both on the Pacific Ring of Fire, but they have very different building standards, so the survival advice gap is a real public health issue, and I’m happy that this is being addressed with infrastructure that already exists and doesn’t really need any extra upkeep since they’re being used all the time. Egg carton reuse Arielle: The next solution is titled “Six smart things to do with an empty egg carton before you toss it in the recycling bin”. Before you toss your next empty egg carton, hear me out. Those 12 little cups, or 10 or six, depending on how many eggs you get, they turn out to be surprisingly useful around the house, and the seed-starting one especially. So that’s one of the uses that I’m going to get into. You just fill each cup with soil, you plant your seeds in them, and then when it’s time, just plant the whole thing into the ground, and then the cardboard breaks down, and the roots never get disturbed. So that would be something that I would do if I had a garden. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Another one that I liked was the jewelry organization thing. So you can create little cups for your jewelry, and right now, all of my jewelry is just, like, willy-nilly all over the place in different rooms in tangles. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: So I don’t need a garden to do that one, so maybe I will try that one out. Karissa: Yeah, I, I love this, and there’s really a big momentum around reducing household waste without buying more eco products, and this is about using what you already have. Japanese sweet potatoes Arielle: The next solution is titled “What sets Japanese sweet potatoes apart, nutritionally speaking?” Japanese sweet potatoes are those, like… They just look like sweet potatoes, but they’re generally kind of longer, I find, and they look purple on the outside, and then when you cut them open, they’re white on the inside. And it turns out that even though they are still sweet potatoes, they are doing completely different things nutritionally than the ones, like the orange ones that so many of us know and love. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And the comparison is more interesting than you’d expect. Japanese sweet potatoes are higher in vitamin C and E and anthocyanins, the same pigments that make blueberries and red cabbage dark, while orange ones are the beta carotene champions. They’re complementary, not interchangeable. The fiber content is about four grams per serving, which puts them in, like, a genuinely filling territory for a carb. And luckily, there’s no evidence-based recommendation for how many to eat per week, so you don’t necessarily need to limit yourself if you end up really, really loving Japanese sweet potatoes. The only thing is that dieticians say, um, make sure you don’t, like, hyper-fixate on them, just like on any food, and don’t make them your only kind of vegetable. Have you tried Japanese sweet potatoes before, Karissa? Karissa: Honestly, I don’t think I have. And I’m kind of not the biggest fan of just, like, normal sweet potatoes either, so they’re okay, but, like, I… And if they’re out, like, at a restaurant or something, like, and you know, it’s in front of me, I’ll eat it, but I usually, like… I, I never feel like preparing it myself. But maybe I’ll give Japanese sweet potatoes a try, and maybe I’ll fall in love with them. Overwintering bees Arielle: The last solution that we are going to share with everyone today is titled “What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees”. This could be considered a counterintuitive one, but maybe not so counterintuitive for longtime Optimists. The best thing you can do for native bees this fall is put down the rake. All that scraggly stuff you’re about to tidy away, the leaf piles, the hollow stems, the dead-looking cane fruit, that’s where the bees love to be. There are over 3,600 native bee species in the US, and most aren’t honey bees. It’s those solitary wild bees that are in steep decline, and most of them nest in your garden over winter. So don’t compost your cut stems in fall. If bees have already nested inside them, composting kills the larvae still developing in there, and I did not know that. I didn’t realize that there’s, like, little baby bees… inside cut stems. Also, try not to worry yourself about the bare patches of dirt in your lawn if you have them. I know it might look like neglected land, but that’s prime bee nesting habitat, apparently. Ground-nesting bees need bare, un-compacted soil to excavate their nests. Karissa: Wow, I didn’t even realize that there were that many, uh, bee species in the US for one, but, um… native bee decline is an issue that feels kind of, uh, abstract until you realize that the solution is literally just doing less yard work, and I love that because- Mm. Yeah … working in the yard can be such a pain. Arielle: Yeah, I mean, I kinda wish I had one. But it can be, uh, it can be toilsome. And maybe the solution sounds familiar to some people… because we have covered No Mow May before, and I think there have been a few articles about, like, just not raking so much in the fall. Yeah. Um, ’cause that doesn’t just help bees, but it also helps other insects and critters that are important for the ecosystem. Quote & Outro Karissa: Well, Arielle, that was a great roundup of solutions, and before we head off for today, we have a positive quote to leave you off with. Arielle: This one is by Robert Frost, and it is, “The best way out is always through.” Karissa: Simple. Arielle: So yes, that’s, uh, yeah, nice and simple, but hard to do sometimes when you’re faced with a situation that you kinda wanna get out of, but you just have to endure and go through it. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Uh, but yeah. Well, on that note, Karissa and I wish all of you a very happy weekend, and we will be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, stay optimistic. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript October 16th, 2026— Flu is already spreading: why October is the window to get vaccinated, plus nine more solutions first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them. A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels —without sacrificing the harvest. Agrivoltaic schemes— putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California . Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs. But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses. A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity. Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants. The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower. This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Soil, Seeds, and Student Power: How Four Canadian Schools are Tackling Food Sovereignty Reading Time: 3 minutes Four schools across Canada show what happens when students are given the tools and trust to build a greenhouse. If you didn’t know it already, students are extremely capable humans, able to tackle projects with a sense of audacity and creativity that (maybe) goes untapped in some older folks. So, when you give them the challenge of growing their own food, they commit, rather wholeheartedly, we should add. It starts as a project, like a club idea, a class assignment, or a response to a funding opportunity, and it becomes something a bit harder to name. A sense of ownership. A connection to where food actually comes from. A reason to show up after school and get dirt under their fingernails. Across four very different Canadian communities, that shift is happening in greenhouses and vertical farms that students built, maintain, and call their own. The Earthlings Climate Club at Sussex Middle School didn’t start big. Five students shared a frustration: nobody at their school was really talking about climate change, so they came up with the idea of building a greenhouse for their breakfast club. The club grew as more students joined, not always because of climate passion, but because their friends were there and it was fun. Those students became advocates too. That’s the lesson the Earthlings want other schools to know: not everyone arrives through the front door of environmental concern, and that’s fine. While waiting for greenhouse materials to arrive (a familiar patience test for rural schools), the students launched a composting program to keep momentum going, earning them a feature in the Telegraph Journal . The greenhouse eventually came together, growing produce for a breakfast club that many students depend on, with ambitions to expand into the cafeteria and local food banks. “Physical hands-on is definitely what I learn through mostly,” said student lead Lyla, “and I feel like we should do more hands-on because it’s way easier to learn.” This next project was never just about the vegetables. For the Ahtahkakoop Cree Nation in Saskatchewan , the greenhouse is one piece of a longer project to rebuild food sovereignty—a way of life that sustained communities for generations before it was systematically disrupted. Youth project lead Jana Sasakamoose framed it quite bluntly: “Many members only get $300 a month to survive off of… It’s hard to meet those needs, let alone basic needs such as food.” Alert Bay students at work building their outdoor greenhouse with the help of First Nations community partners. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . The response was a greenhouse dome chosen for its ability to maximize natural light and air circulation, selected after community consultations on preferred features and plant varieties. Over 250 community members were engaged through canning workshops, gardening sessions, and planning conversations. This is a multi-phase project, with solar panels, underground food storage, and ongoing education all in the pipeline. Alert Bay sits on a small island off the coast of British Columbia, accessible only by ferry. Everything comes by boat, including all the school’s food. With 34 students, 98% of whom are First Nations, and relentlessly windy, rainy weather, a conventional outdoor garden was never going to work. What the school had, though, was community knowledge. Indigenous nations on the island, including the Kwakwaka’wakw, ‘Namgis, and Nawalakw, had already been greenhouse farming, and students came to school with that experience from home. Rather than starting from scratch, Alert Bay Elementary asked its First Nations partners for guidance on suppliers, building techniques, and growing approaches suited to the island’s conditions. The result is a student-maintained greenhouse feeding the school’s hot lunch program, built on the principle of learning from what’s already working. “If we start now,” said student lead Evan, “we can make a difference in the way our school and community think about food and waste.” Oilfields High School in Diamond Valley, Alberta, has been running a vertical farm out of a modified shipping container for years, growing microgreens, lettuce, and herbs that students sell to local grocers, restaurants, and their own school concession. The problem was pests. Before the N:OW for Net-Zero funded biosecurity headerhouse was built, the farm lost 30% of its crops to contamination. Since construction (done by hand with shop students and retired local tradespeople), that loss rate has hit zero. Students at Oilfields High School surround the adult lead, Cindy Watts, as they prep to sell their school-grown microgreens to their student body at lunch. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . CTV News Calgary and CBC have covered the farm , and in April 2026, their Member of Parliament, John Barlow, visited to recognize the students’ work firsthand. This year, the farm launched microgreen smoothies at the school concession twice a week, earned a local grocer’s support for purchasing the school’s greens, and is now actively recruiting youth volunteers and exploring university and company sponsorships to support students as they transition out of high school. A greenhouse, a dome, a modified shipping container, and a grow light in a boot room. The form changes, but the impulse is the same: students decide that food sovereignty isn’t someone else’s problem to solve, and they get to work. The post Soil, Seeds, and Student Power: How Four Canadian Schools are Tackling Food Sovereignty appeared first on Happy Eco News .
