items.descriptionOriginal: J ust as President Joe Biden was showing signs of cognitive decline so conspicuous that he was compelled to drop out of the presidential race in 2024, my own father’s dementia was worsening. He lived with us, and yet he lived in another reality entirely. One where he no longer understood that the food on his plate was his, and the food on my daughter’s was hers. One where he grew agitated when we wouldn’t let him walk in a rainstorm. One where he no longer knew my name. Being in the bizarre world of his deteriorating mind was not unlike reading the headlines each day as the months, and then years, went on. My once sweet and Buddhist dad’s abandonment of norms, his misplaced anger, his seemingly selfish relentlessness, were a product of his disease — the nerve cells in his brain were no longer communicating properly. His context for just about everything fell away. Courtney and her father at Thanksgiving. Credit: John Cary The country’s deterioration was different, a deliberate poisoning more than an organic disease, but the parallels were there. It felt pathological how callous and hard our country had become. But there was also something happening underneath my dad’s deterioration. My whole family was learning to collectively care for him — taking him on drives and scream-singing Tom Petty when he would get sundowners (a medical term for late-day confusion in dementia patients), reading Pema Chödrön aloud to him in the backyard, letting him have our ice cream cones when he would reach for them. And our neighbors were in on the tenderness. They’d call when he wandered too far or help him back home when they found him sitting in their unlocked cars. In our local park, when my dad started helping himself to a plate of sandwiches meticulously arranged on a picnic table, the Japanese family they belonged to welcomed this unkempt, white, six-foot-two stranger to their outing as if he were a long lost relative. Likewise, there has been something happening underneath the deterioration of our country. While the headlines reveal the truth of the matter — data centers bulldozing their way into rural communities, masked federal agents yanking delivery workers off their bikes, industry lobbyists buying legislation that allows them to poison our water and air — there are also young people planting community gardens to tackle gun violence in Milwaukee, Wisconsin; caregivers riding their kids to school in bike buses in Montclair, New Jersey; and folks of all ages gathering for the Black Joy Parade in Oakland, California. While some national figures are trying to flood the zone with so much chaos that we can’t keep up, other Americans are working hard to bring running water and indoor plumbing to those who still don’t have it. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] We’re witnessing a reweaving of local fabric, and a renewed curiosity in one another. Parents watching the resurgence of blatant misogyny are intentionally raising boys who embrace their tender feelings and connections. Famously red Texas has had more data center protests than any other state , so perhaps there is more possibility for labor and climate collaboration than we have understood. Leaders in a wide range of faiths weathered the bitter cold of Minneapolis to join local solidarity protests against ICE raids after the tragic death of Renée Good. It seems we are curious again about what role faith might play in our ethical lives together, how we can build a culture of mutual aid in our very unequal communities, and even how we might better understand the economic pain of those who have been abandoned and stereotyped by mainstream media and the political elite. If the last decade or two has been about expanding our horizons, it feels like this one is becoming about humbly narrowing the aperture on our lives and trying to get right with our neighbors, housed and unhoused alike. At a time when A.I. threatens to unravel us in so many ways, economist E.F. Schumacher’s wisdom from his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful: Economics as if People Mattered feels worth reviving: “I have no doubt that it is possible to give a new direction to technological development, a direction that shall lead it back to the real needs of man, and that also means: To the actual size of man. Man is small, and, therefore, small is beautiful.” In the end, this is what saved my family as we took care of my dad; the small moments in the midst of the chaos where we could register his essence intact, where we could devote ourselves to the sacred practice of showing up for him even when it was hard, when we could rest in the awe of it all. It didn’t cure his illness, but it reminded us of us — the fabric, the tenderness, the main thing. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime I wish that same reminder for our country in the months and years ahead — a way to keep our eye on the systemic harm, while keeping our hands in the dirt of our own communities. There are people in our midst who have lost their way through deep delusion, but there are also better angels: The family that offers a strange old man a sandwich; the organizers fighting for clean water for everyone, no exceptions; the daughters of the revolution baking casseroles for the undocumented families hiding in an attic room of their Minneapolis neighbors’ homes. May we never turn away from the systemic injustice, but may we also turn towards the small and beautiful. It’s all real and deeply interconnected, and deserves our fierce attention. items.descriptionOriginal: I f you’re anything like us, you’re not exactly in a congenial mood right now. With the U.S. midterm elections fewer than three weeks away, you might be feeling combat-ready. And who could blame you? Seemingly on the ballot: the very future of the republic, steered by leaders who will shape policy about the climate, A.I., immigration, affordability, wars and many other critical issues. There’s a lot at stake. And yet, for many of us, the way we feel goes beyond those stakes. One part of our brain chugs along analytically, taking stances on legislation, policy and governance. Meanwhile, another part seethes with contempt for those who disagree: They must be stupid, immoral, blind to the facts. Multiply by 340 million, and election season becomes a volatile brew. But there’s hope. While social media algorithms, elected officials, and yes, even our own friends and colleagues, encourage us to close ranks and shut out dissenting voices, others are working in the other direction: reaching out, listening deeply, locating points of connection where they exist, and turning toward those they disagree with, rather than away. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] From now through Election Day, these are the people we’ll journey with. We’ll meet liberals and conservatives who are joining forces despite their differences to oppose data centers and border walls. We’ll talk to students who are turning their college campuses into spaces that welcome an array of opinions, and others participating in cultural exchanges far from their hometowns and comfort zones. We’ll listen in on conversations between “deep canvassers” and the voters they’re hearing out. And we’ll learn how polarization takes hold of the brain — and how, little by little, we can loosen its grip. The Depolarization Project isn’t a call to meet in the middle — it’s an experiment in curiosity. What forces fuel our sense of tribalism? Why do opposing perspectives register as a threat? Can we be open to differences of opinion without compromising our values? Is there hope for those of us who harbor a secret desire to bridge the divides? We know many of you may be skeptical. We hope you’ll take this journey with us regardless, and learn whether we can we fight for what we believe in without closing our minds and our hearts. Illustration by MUTI The post Welcome to the Depolarization Project appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Scientists Develop a Seaweed Coating to Extend the Freshness of Fruit Reading Time: 3 minutes A new seaweed coating can keep strawberries fresher at room temperature than even a refrigerator, offering a lower-carbon way to fight food waste. A new seaweed coating can keep fresh fruit lasting longer than even a refrigerator can. Researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC) developed the edible dip. In tests, coated strawberries stayed fresh at room temperature for four days or more. Uncoated strawberries left at room temperature molded within just two days. Even refrigerated, untreated berries started molding by day four regardless. Coated strawberries kept in the fridge lasted a full six days, the longest result recorded in the study. The seaweed coating relies on agar, a substance pulled from red algae. Agar is already a common food additive and a popular vegan substitute for gelatin. On its own, though, agar simply forms a thick, unremarkable gel. Doctoral student Ivy Chiu led the study alongside senior researcher Tianxi Yang at UBC. The two published their findings in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry in August 2026. Their team says no one had combined these particular ingredients into a coating like this before. Everything changed once researchers added zinc and tannic acid to the mix. Zinc is an essential nutrient, and tannic acid occurs naturally in grapes and tea. Together with agar, these ingredients self-assembled into tiny, evenly spread microparticles. That self-assembly surprised even the research team studying it. The particles form a thin, clear film that seals in moisture and blocks gas exchange. The coating also carries antibacterial and antioxidant properties that further slow spoilage. A seaweed coating enhanced with zinc and tannic acid self-assembles into a thin, clear film of evenly spread microparticles that seals in moisture, blocks gas exchange, and delivers antibacterial and antioxidant properties that slow food spoilage in ways the research team itself did not anticipate. Photo by Clare Kiernan, courtesy of the University of British Columbia . Researchers describe watching the mixture transform from a cloudy liquid into a uniform layer. The process happens within minutes once all three ingredients combine in solution. Dipped fruit emerges with a coating so thin it dries almost invisible. Cut apple slices treated with the seaweed coating stayed fresh for about 24 hours. Untreated slices, by comparison, began visibly decaying within 12 hours. Coated grapes lasted almost 14 days, a full week longer than untreated fruit. Across all three fruits, the coating roughly doubled shelf life compared to no treatment. Weight loss at the four-day mark dropped from 30% down to 13%. Treated fruit also kept more of its vitamin C and antioxidant content. Safety testing found no signs of toxicity in human intestinal cells. Researchers say the coating is safe to eat and washes off easily. It also preserves the fruit’s normal nutritional value throughout storage. A lifecycle analysis compared the coating’s environmental footprint to standard refrigeration. Emissions from the seaweed coating came in lower than or equal to those from cold storage. Researchers say these modest savings could add up across an entire supply chain. Reducing spoilage matters most in a food system that wastes enormous amounts of produce. Nearly half of all food produced in Canada is lost or wasted every year. That waste costs the Canadian economy an estimated $58 billion annually. Fresh fruits and vegetables are especially prone to this kind of loss. They lose moisture quickly and become vulnerable to mold soon after harvest. Long supply chains that rely heavily on refrigeration add further cost and emissions along the way. Cutting down on refrigeration could also ease strain on energy grids. Maintaining cold temperatures from farm to store demands significant infrastructure and power. A coating like this could reduce that demand at several points along the supply chain. They are also testing the seaweed coating across a wider range of fruits and vegetables. The team describes their invention as a practical strategy for building more resilient produce supply chains. Cutting food waste at this scale could ease pressure on refrigeration-heavy supply chains everywhere. A simple seaweed coating might not replace the fridge completely. But it could give fresh produce a longer, greener path from farm to table. The post Scientists Develop a Seaweed Coating to Extend the Freshness of Fruit appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A bleached coral, stripped of its color and slowly starving, can come back to life in just seven weeks -- if it is placed in contact with a healthy twin. Researchers at Stanford University recently discovered that when genetically identical coral fragments touch, their tissues fuse into what scientist Danny Collins calls "a nutrient highway," and within as little as 36 hours, life-giving algae begin flowing from the healthy fragment into the dying one. The discovery began with a happy accident: a healthy coral slipped against a bleached one in a tank, and someone was paying close enough attention to notice what happened next. The finding won't save coral reefs overnight -- the technique only works between genetic clones, and the ocean keeps warming, which causes coral to bleach. But the findings do open a door. Collins and his team are now exploring whether the algae themselves can be extracted and introduced to bleached corals at scale, without needing the physical bridge at all. While he is clear-eyed about the limits: the real solution is being able to stop coral bleaching in the first place, the horizons feel brighter: "bleached corals aren't a lost cause," he offers.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall there’s a pull to tidy things up. Cut back the perennials, rake the leaves, clear the beds, put the garden to rest. It feels satisfying, honestly, and spring does seem to start from a cleaner place. The thing is, all that leaf litter, those hollow stems, those patches of scraggly dead plant matter? That’s where the bees are. Over 3,600 bee species are native to the United States, and most of them are not honey bees. It’s the native wild bees, including mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, long-horned bees, bumble bees, and hundreds of others, that are in steep decline. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest, lays her eggs, stocks them with food, seals them up, and dies. As Matthew Shepherd , Director of Outreach and Education at the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation , explains, the offspring “complete most of their life stages in the cell, remaining there until the following year, when they emerge at the same season their mother was active.” That nest is almost certainly somewhere in your garden. Sam Droege , Wildlife Biologist at the USGS, says wild bees are nesting above ground and in the ground somewhere nearby no matter where you live. Ecological landscape designer Kim Eierman puts it plainly: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Most of what they need is already there, and the beauty of this solution is that all you have to do is less. What to do with the fallen leaves Move them rather than bag them. Bumble bee queens hibernate by digging a few inches underground or into leaf mulch, so piling leaves onto flower beds or into a back corner of the yard makes them a winter home. Leaf piles also give fireflies and other small garden creatures a place to wait out the cold. Shepherd’s guidance: remove leaves from anywhere they’re a slip hazard or blocking a drain, but keep them on flower borders, along the base of a hedge, or tucked into a back corner. A rake or broom does the job without the disturbance a leaf blower causes. Think twice before cutting everything back Pruning everything to the ground in fall can cost wild bees their winter home. “Avoiding the typical fall cleanup on plants and keeping stems of perennials and annuals creates nesting opportunities for tunnel-nesting bees such as small carpenter bees and leafcutters,” Shepherd says. The birds appreciate it too; they’ll forage on the seedheads through winter. If a tidy front yard matters to you, Droege has a workable compromise: cut back to about a foot tall instead of to the ground. “A plant needs to be damaged or dead for bees to be able to use it,” he says, so a shorter cut still creates usable nesting structure without looking neglected. If you’re already mid-cleanup, don’t compost what you’ve cut. “If any bees are already nesting in the stems, composting them will cause the end of that cycle,” Droege says. A loose pile left on the ground or behind the shed keeps the cycle going. Eierman adds that pithy stems from elderberry, raspberry, hydrangea, and Joe Pye weed are especially useful to cavity-nesting bees and can be bundled and left in place through winter. Leave brush piles, snags, and cane fruit stems Pruned branches can go into a brush pile rather than the compost. Loose piles don’t do much; Eierman notes they need to be “fairly tight and dense, providing cavities that shelter bees from rain.” Dead or dying trees are candidates for keeping if they’re well away from the house. These are called snags. They develop hollow passages over time as beetles tunnel through the dead wood, and cavity-nesting bees use those passages the following season. A snag that’s too tall to feel comfortable about can be cut back to a manageable height without losing what makes it useful. For cane fruits like raspberries, blackberries, and boysenberries, Droege says the same logic applies. “Cane fruits only fruit in year two,” he says. “Instead of cutting them to the ground, trimming them to a foot tall provides the best nesting material for a whole series of native wild bees.” Leave bare patches of soil undisturbed Most native bees nest in the ground and need bare, uncompacted soil to excavate their nests. “Don’t try to repair all the bare ground — leave the open areas, as bees like to nest there,” says Droege. Sandy or loamy soil in a sunny spot is ideal, but even a few square feet counts. If a bare patch feels too sparse, Eierman says planting very sparsely may still leave enough exposed soil between plants; just skip the mulch or landscape fabric, as both block bees from getting in. Treat it as wild habitat rather than an incomplete garden bed: no tilling, no cleaning up, not even in spring. Keep some flowers going through fall Most bees have wrapped up their nesting cycle by the time temperatures drop, but sweat bees and mining bees are still out foraging late in the season. Goldenrod and asters are the flowers they’re looking for. Having something in bloom through fall, and building toward a range of bloom times from spring through the end of the season, gives different species something to work with at different points in the year. “Expanding your garden for next spring and reducing your lawn is the biggest thing you can do for wild bees ,” Droege says. Eierman says it best: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Leave the leaves. Don’t compost the stems. Keep a corner wild. That’s most of it. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary .
